The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 164) to amend the Act of 1S99, respecting the city of Ottawa. He said : Mr. Speaker, I thought at one time of making a proposal with the view of consolidating the work of the Ottawa Improvement Commission and the Ottawa Parks Committee, a body under the control of the city of Ottawa, or, a body that has recently been abolished, and its powers transferred to the city of Ottawa by an Ontario Act. However, I realize that at the present stage of the session we would hardly have time to deliberate upon a measure of that kind. The amendment I propose now is merely to enlarge the number of the commission, without in any way changing its powers or responsibilities. It is proposed that there shall be added four commissioners to those already appointed. The object is to broaden the scope of the commission. It is not intended that all these gentlemen shall be from the city of Ottawa, but the design is to take some gentlemen from outside the city of Ottawa, and perhaps some hon. gentlemen sitting in parliament, who have an interest in the national capital, and who will have sufficient leisure to enable them to assist in its improvement. I do not anticipate tuat there will be any objection. If there is, I quite realize that any Bill at this stage will not get through.
Is it the Governor in Council who appoints the additional number of commissioners ?
Yes.

Before this motion is carried, I would like to draw the attention of the government to the fact that on the 14th day of this session there was supposed to have been a detailed statement brought down to this House concerning the expenditure of this Improvement Commission. It does strike me that the section of the Act requiring this return has not been complied with. I have here a statement as brought down by the commission, and it is not a detailed statement at all. It is not a detailed statement, as the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) will see, by comparing it with the re-

quirements of section 11 of the Act. This section reads :
The commission shall render to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General and to the corporation, on or before the first day of September in each year, detailed statements of aJll their receipts and expenditures up to the last day of June in such year ; and copies of such statements shall be laid before parliament by the Minister of Finance and Receiver General within the first fourteen days of the next following session thereof.
I have the statement here, and although it involves something like $92,000, it does not give the names of the streets that the money has been expended upon. I will read the list that it gives.
Princess Terrace, King street, printing and advertising, Concession and other streets, stationery and office supplies, telephone, rent and storage, Rideau River bridges, road machinery, Ri-deau canal driveway and parks, Rideau street, Keefer property, tools, implements, &c., Wellington street, Bank street, McKay and other streets.
It is due to this. parliament that we should know upon what streets the money is being expended. I did take occasion, when the estimates were before this House, to make some inquiries in connection with this expenditure, and I find that I have been greatly misunderstood. The ' Journal,' of this city, which seems to take great interest in the few remarks I made on that occasion, accuses me of having been loaded up by some disgruntled Liberals of this city, but to clear the mind of the editor of the ' Journal,' let me say that I have not had any conversation with any disgruntled Liberal in this city or outside of this city regarding this question. I have had. no conversation with any of them in connection with this matter, and I am not here for the purpose of cleaning the decks of hon. gentlemen opposite.
It is the duty of the members of this parliament to inquire into an expenditure involving $00,000 a year. If we desire to make this the Washington of the North, it is just as much our duty to consider a matter of this kind as it is the duty of the ' Journal ' newspaper of the city of Ottawa. What I did on that occasion I believe was my duty. I for one am not opposing this expenditure, but I am opposed to this Star Chamber method of doing business. I believe this money should be expended in a business-like manner, as all public money should be expended, and it was for that reason I rose to object to certain things being done by this Improvement Commission. I have been here for a number of years, and I have watched carefully some of the improvements made in the streets of Ottawa, and I wish to say I believe this expenditure could be put to better uses. I have heard rumours going around this city in connection with this expenditure, and one would have to be deaf if he did not hear them. For my part, should I occupy a seat in the House, I intend to pay a little more
attention to this expenditure in years to come. I ask that a more detailed statement of the expenditure of that money be laid before parliament, in order that we may have a chance of sizing up exactly how it is expended. We can criticise the general estimates submitted to parliament, but we have no opportunity in this case of criticising the expenditure unless an amendment is made to the Act. A detailed statement is brought down within the first fourteen days of the session, and that is the only statement upon which we can hope to give the matter fair criticism. I wish to point out that in giving the expenditure a fair criticism, I do so not for the purpose of opposing it, but in order to ensure that the money is not improperly expended.

Although it is not usual to debate the question on the introduction of a Bill, yet I wish to make a few remarks. I have heard it said on thoroughly good authority that this commission transacted business behind closed doors. I regard that as entirely wrong. If there is nothing done which is improper, then they need not be ashamed to have their proceedings open to the public. I agree with the proposition to increase the number of the commissioners, because if the information we have is anything like correct, the whole work is done by one or two individuals, and the disclosures which took place under the late mayor showed a state of things which is anything but proper. My memory is, that one of the commissioners who is largely controlling the business was furnishing the supplies himself ; that practically the money was expended where ever he desired ; that it was expended upon streets where it was in the interests of himself and others that it should be expended, and that in reality the money which parliament voted for the purpose of improving the streets of Ottawa was practically put in the pockets of the commissioners by dealing with themselves through fictitious names. The statement is made that they were enabled to do this largely because of the smallness of the commission. It is, therefore, important that the commission should be enlarged and that some one outside of the corporation should have the authority to appoint the additional commissioner that it is proposed to put on that board.

I may say that when the gentlemen upon this Ottawa Improvement Commission were appointed I did not know a single one of them personally, and I am not sure that I have known any of them since except that I have once or twice spoken to Mr. Bate and Mr. Cunningham. I have no special acquaintance with the details of their work, but I think I can say that if hon. gentlemen made an examination of it and drove over the work which

has been done, they would say that it would be impossible to do better work or more work for the amount of money expended. That, after all, is the purpose that the government and parliament have in view in the constitution of the commission and its appointment. I am quite satisfied that 1 can safely say that the government and parliament can congratulate themselves upon the fact, that the work undertaken by the commission has been most successfully and most efficiently done. There has been no waste of any kind whatever. There was some discussion in the local press, but if my hon. friend fallows that discussion 1 think they will find that it arose largely from the jealousy between different municipal bodies, which under the circumstances may readily be understood. A close examination of the matter will, I think, show my hon. friends that there is no doubt but that the Ottawa Improvement Commission got first-class value for every dollar of money it expended, and that it would be quite impossible for anybody however constituted to get any better value than they got.

speechtext: May I have the consent of the House to say one or two words more. It was brought out in that examination that load after load of stones was brought around the streets of the city time after time, and the same load weighed and charged to that account and paid for. It was also brought out that materials which went on the streets belonged to one of the commissioners, was taken out of a storehouse of his own under another name, and that it was traced back that it was really sold by the commissioner himself.

I do not sympathize with the view that the public press should be admitted to every meeting of every public body. There are hundreds of cases where the admission of the press, even to meetings of bodies of a public character, may not be advantageous to the public, and I believe that the best journalists of the country will approve of that view. There is no use generalizing in this matter ; we must take each case as it comes up. Let me point out to the hon. member (Mr. Ingram) that if there was any exception to be taken to the details which were furnished in the statement required by the statute, if the hon. gentleman had called attention to it at an earlier stage of the session I would have been very glad to look into it and see if there was any cause for complaint.

When we were discussing the estimates for the Maria street bridge I called the hon. gentleman's attention to it, and the hon. gentleman said: We had better allow that to stand over as I propose to amend the Bill, and when that comes up it will be the proper time to discuss this question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Certainly it is the proper time, but if the hon. gentleman wanted to complain that any information brought down was defective, the proper time to complain was at an earlier stage of the session when we could make it good, which we cannot do now. In the Act respecting the Ottawa Improvement Commission it is required that the accounts should be audited in the same manner as the accounts of any public department. Every item of the expenditure of that commission is fully set forth in the report of the Auditor-General-as fully as it could have been if it had been the direct expenditure of any department of the government. If the hon. gentleman turns to page G-31 of the Auditor General's report he will find six pages filled with all the details of the expenditure of the Ottawa Improvement Commission down to the last cent.
Then, I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman that the statement which he is supposed to receive from that commission is required to be laid before this House.

I had great pleasure in placing that statement before the House as contained within the four corners of this admirable blue-book on almost the first day of the session, and if my hon. friend has not had his attention drawn to it, it only goes to show that he does not value this book as highly as I do. I do not object to any fair criticism ; but I do regret that at this stage of the session observations are made reflecting on the good faith of the members of the commission. I have no special knowledge of the work of the commission other than that which I get from the public reports ; and, while I have a great admiration for the press, and while as an old journalist I should be the last to speak disparagingly of the press, yet I do not think my hon. friend should accept everything that appears in the press as absolutely certain. As the whole matter involved in this Bill is a mere addition to the number of the commissioners, t admit that the discussion upon it might as well take place on the first reading ; and if objection is not to be taken to the Bill itself, I hope lion, gentlemen will not too hastily assume that statements which appear in the public press reflecting on the commission are correct until we can have an opportunity of inquiring into them before the Public Accounts Committee.
Is the hon. minister in favour of keeping the press excluded from the meetings of that commission ?

I would
reserve my judgment as to that ; but I
would be inclined to think I am.

I cannot allow this occasion to pass without expressing my regret that the hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken should on mere street rumour felt themselves called upon to repeat in this House statements which are not only very much exaggerated, but which have been shown to be without any foundation. I do not think the gentlemen who compose this commission-such men as Mr. Henry Bate, Mr. Cunningham and Mr. Riopelle-who have very generously during the last three years given their services gratuitously to the work of the commission, will thank these lion, gentlemen for having made themselves the mouthpieces of these street corner talks, which amount to nothing.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman :	is it true that one of
these commissioners threatened to resign unless the business was transacted in a different manner ?

I do not know anything about that ; but I know that these gentlemen have done good service and have received absolutely nothing for it. One of these commissioners, Mr. Riopelle, during the whole of the last working season personally superintended the work. He was on the ground day after day during the whole time the men were there, giving his services without any remuneration whatever. I think it is a very poor recompense to these men, who have shown such public spirit, to be treated in the way hon. gentlemen opposite have treated them. The only statement made, to which the hon. member for East Grey has referred, and which, like all other stories, gets bigger as it is repeated, is that a tender of some relative of one of the commissioners for furnishing cement has been accepted.
Was that not charged in one of the public newspapers in the city of Ottawa ?

I do not know. I do not follow all that the newspapers say, and I do not attach the same importance that the hon. gentleman does to what appears in them. If that charge was made, it should have been investigated ; I do not know why it wa's not. I do not think there is any truth in it. But I am not directing my attention to that. What I am finding fault with is that gentlemen who have given their services to the public for nothing should be treated in this way. If there is any accusation to be brought against any one of them, it is only fair and just that it should be properly made and investigated, and that mere street rumours should not be repeated in this House, and amplified and exaggerated in the way these statements have been to-day.

I want to ask the hon. member if he supposes that the statement
I made was exaggerated. I gave it exactly as it was given to me by a reliable and respectable citizen of Ottawa, and I gave it as nearly as I could in his own words ; and, so far as I can judge, I believe the. statement to be correct.

House in committee on Bill (No. 149) to amend the Land Titles Act, 1894.-The Minister of the Interior.
On section 1,
What has been the custom in dealing with. lands belonging to a second party ?

The only change made in this section is to settle a question with regard to a power of attorney. Where a general power of attorney has been given there was a difference of opinion as to whether that prevented the owner from dealing with the land himseif while the power of attorney was in existence. The hon. gentleman is aware that in the province of Ontario you can give a general power of attorney to John Smith to deal with your land, and you can still sign or deal with it yourself. This docs not interfere with that power. Under the Torrens system, when a power of attorney was given, the land had to be specifically described in every case. Then we introduced in Manitoba, and subsequently into the territories, the idea of a general power of attorney, as under the old system. Then cases arose in which the judges expresssed the opinion that the giving of a general power of attorney excluded the right of the owner to deal with the property until the general, power of attorney was cancelled. This provision is to clear up any doubt.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

I see that the main estimates for 1901-1902 amounted on revenue account to $48,826,878.16, and on capital account to $11,097,8G2.71. Then, we have supplementary estimates down, amounting to $1,358,683.70, and further supplementary estimates amounting to $4,189,245.07. These supplementary estimates provide for sums required to carry on the expenses of the country up to the 30th June this year. These sums make a grand total expenditure voted for this year to carry on the affairs of the country of $65,472,609.54. If the hon. gentlemen had kept their promises, they could have run the country as efficiently as the late Conservative government did on $38,000,000 or $39,000,000, and they should have saved this year $25,000,000 out of the revenues of the country, and had $10,000,000 to spare besides. If they had done that it would not have been necessary for the hon. Minister of Finance to borrow money. They have sunk the country in debt. I suppose that having such a buoyant revenue last year the hon. gentlemen felt justified in spending on consolidated fund and capital account nearly sixty-five and a half million dollars. They promised to carry on the affairs of the country for $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 less than the late government were carrying on the affairs of the country, when all they required to spend was from $38,000,000 to $41,000,000, including both consolidated fund and capital account. If hon. gentleman had kept their word, the revenue would have been coming in all the same, and they could have paid off our debt, and have had sufficient money to have carried on the affairs of the country, and saved $10,000, 000 or $12,000,000 a year to pay off our mortgage debt. They should have done that, but in place of that, all the money has been spent. Here is this sixty-five and a half million which has been spent this year, and hon. gentlemen opposite cannot point to any permanent improvement other than those which are usually made, notwithstanding this enormous expenditure. They are spending $65,000,000, paying two or three times what they should for taking the census, and allowing the money to be frittered away, while they cannot point to any Canadian Pacific Railway or large improvement such as was carried out by the Conservative government. Yet, in the face of all this, they are coming and asking power to borrow more money, with the object of increasing our expenditure, instead of decreasing it.

Mr. Speaker, before going into Supply, I wish to make a few remarks on what I consider a very important subject, and before I take my seat I shall close with a resolution. A few weeks ago, in the city of Woodstock, Oxford county, while attending a meeting of the Dairymen's Association of Western Canada, I made a few remoras on this most important subject, a subject which I consider of the greatest and most vital importance to the welfare of the people of Canada. It is not necessary for me to tell the hon. members of this House, or the people of this Dominion, what that subject is, as we all know that the transportation problem is the greatest question which the people of Canada have to grapple with, have to solve, and have staring them in the face at the present moment. It is not my desire to take up much of the time of the House in discussing this very important question, and I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I have been compelled, on account of my health being somewhat impaired during the
last few weeks, to delay bringing this matter before the House at an earlier date. But, better late than never. The subject which I intend to discuss is that of utilizing the natural waterways of this Dominion for transporting our products to the seaboard.
It is not my intention to condemn the government, neither is it my intention to abuse or condemn the great railways of the Dominion for not having given us better accommodation and better rates of freiguc for carrying our goods, but it is my intention to ask this House, and to ask the country, to throw politics aside and go to work to do something to place the producers and manufacturers of this country in a position whereby they can place the products of the farm, the sea, the mines and the forests on the markets of the world at as cheap a rate of freight as that of our neighbours to the south, or for that matter, of any other country in the world. Up to the present moment we have been paying very much higher rates on everything we produce than they are paying in the United States. Over there they are utilizing their waterways for all they are worth during the season of navigation. They are also utilizing immense elevators and warehouses for storing goods, holding them at their seaports or lake ports until navigation opens, knowing they can get a very much lower rate of freight, while we on this side are practically doing nothing at all along the line of utilizing our waterways from the head of lake Superior and lake Ontario, clean down to the gulf of St. Lawrence. It is my intention, in as few words as possible, to show what the possibilities of our great waterways are, and as hon. members all know, we are now and have been spending large sums of money for the purpose of educating our people how to produce the finest goods. We have our farmers' institutes, our cheese and butter associations, our fat stock shows, our fruit, honey, poultry, swine and breeders' associations, our shows and exhibitions of all kinds, our agricultural colleges, &e., all of which are receiving assistance from the government, doing everything in our power to increase the quantity and improve the quality of our goods. But not a thing but talk, talk, talk, and no action as far as improving our freight rates is concerned. What is the use in spending money in improving the quality of our products, when we are taking no action whatever in trying to solve the transportation problem, which if we could do and place our goods on the markets of the world as cheaply as those of our neighbours to the south of us, we would be receiving millions of dollars more for the producers and manufacturers of this country's goods than we are receiving to-day. We have been talking for years and years of appointing a railway commission. We have had a railway commissioner appointed, but what has been done, or what have we been told ? Not a single thing but what we have known
I)o I understand the hon. gentleman to mean that there is cheese shipped via Portland during the time the port of Montreal is open ?
Oh, yes. Shippers have been compelled* to send it via Portland to escape the high rates of insurance charge via Montreal. I may say that the insurance rates last year were almost prohibitive.
During the summer season ?

Yes, and in consequence many people shipped produce via Portland.
Another point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is that of hauling cheese from different parts of the country to be placed in cold storage at central points, such as Morris-burg, Brockville, Belleville, Ingersoll, Woodstock, London, Stratford, Listowel and other centres. The concentration rates for cheese in the district west of Toronto is based as follows :
From points west of London, and north of the main line of the Grand Trunk 2u| cents per hundred pounds have been charged, and east of London and south of the main line of the Grand Trunk, 18i cents per hundred pounds have been charged. Upon shipping these goods out of store the shipper's rate was based on the through rate via Montreal, receiving on this basis, a rebate of 16J cents per hundred pounds.
For comparison we will take the concentration rates on cheese at cold storage points in the United States, which are based on a much more lenient plan than is the case in Canada. There are many cold storage points in New York state where cheese is concen-

trated on a basis of five cents per hundred pounds, and when the buyer wants to ship his goods out, he has the option of asking the various railways for a rate of freight on his goods to the seaboard, thus getting competition where we have none, and we are obliged to pay the high rate.
I give these figures in the House in order to show to the people of Canada what immense possibilities we have if we will only throw partyism to the winds and work together, and spend a few million dollars in assisting nature to perfect the great waterways which the good Lord has provided us with. In discussing with me the waterways of Canada, a friend of mine from Chicago, who had 4<4 years' experience on American waterways, said that if a corporation were organized for the transportation of western products from Fort William, Fort Arthur, and other Canadian points, and also from Duluth and Chicago to the seaboard of Nova Scotia, it should be as follows :
A steamship line to start with, say comprised of seven or eight 5,000 or 6,000 ton steamers from the points above named to some point on Georgian Bay, thence by rail to Toronto, thence by steamship from Toronto to the Atlantic seaboard. On the eastern division there should be employed at the beginning, or shortly after, twenty-five to thirty steel steamers, full size of the canal locks, beginning at the western end, with the number of steamers above mentioned carrying from 175,000 to 200,000 bushels of grain, equipped with all the modern appliances for the quick handling of all kinds of freight. The eastern terminal of boats, I think, should be Collingwood, where there should be erected a modern elevator ; two elevating legs which would discharge the cargo in about five hours. These two legs should have a capacity of 20,000 bushels per hour, and be similar to those used in Chicago, Buffalo and such large centres. In addition to this, freight sheds for rolling freight and merchandise should be erected, and everything modern connected with the rapid and cheap handling of freight should be installed.
From Collingwood to Toronto the railroad should be an air-line practically, laid with 100-pound Tails, and equipped with 75-ton cars, and Collingwood being more than 300 feet higher than Toronto, the heavy products eastbouud would meet with the downgrade the greater part of the way, excepting one short distance of five or six miles, where the slightest up-grade exists. This speed would be reinforced with an auxiliary engine, thereby enabling one engine to draw immense trains.
Having reached Toronto, a similar elevator to that at Collingwood. with the exception of the elevating legs, which are not required, should be built, and in addition, an elevated trestle should be erected so that trains can be run up this elevation and the cars dumped in the hopper, which should ride the
board of the ship, without the grain passing through an elevator.
With this new system, vessels such as will go through the locks would be loaded in one and one and a half hours, loading about 70,000 bushels of wheat. They will then proceed to Montreal, where another elevator will be erected and kept full of grain. With from 30,000 to 40,000 bushels in the shipping bins, the additional lighterage should complete the cargo of the ship from Toronto, so that at any hour of the day or night when the ship arrives in Montreal, the watchmen could draw this quantity into the ship in from one to one and a half hour's time, the elevator not being required to use any machinery during the putting aboard of the lighterage, as the additional cargo would run by gravitation into the ship. Why this lighterage system would be used is that the ship can only load to 14 feet draught passing through the canal and locks from Toronto to Montreal, while they can be loaded- to their full capacity when they arrive at Montreal, which means about 110,000 bushels. They will then proceed to the eastern terminal down by the sea. An elevator should also be erected there similar to the Collingwood elevator, with two elevating legs, and which would discharge the full cargo in about five hours. This done the ship would immediately pass to the coal trestles or shutes, and with a cargo of coal awaiting her would be dumped into the boat in three or four hours' time. This, with any other local, package or import freight would be put on the twin deck of the ships and carried through" the Gulf, the River St. Lawrence and Lake Ontario, to Toronto or any other way port between the two points.
The Toronto terminal should be equipped with the most modern machinery for the rapid handling of coal cargoes, and with three or four of the modern fast hoists, costing about .$20,000 each. The cargo of 2,000 tons would be taken out in five or six hours' time.
The unloading machinery of this plant should unload three hoists per minute of four and four and a half tons of coal each bucket for each hoist, and three or four hoists unloading will readily determine the result. Fast hoist coal docks should also be established in Montreal.
The further aim of the company should be to have large elevator storage capacity, warehouse and cold storage at the seaboard, whereby shippers of all classes of merchandise may send their goods forward, at a season when they can have suitable markets for such merchandise in Europe. It could be stored at a nominal charge at the seaboard and held there until the dealer or producer thought fit to send it forward to England. In this case it would lie well to have shippers rush their goods forward to the seaboard before the close of navigation, and they could ship them across the ocean any time during the winter months. The

same rule could be applied to imported goods or articles, storing them there during the winter months and forwarding them to all parts in western Canada as soon as navigation opened. My idea would be to build ships suitable to pass through the present canals and locks and to build them with a view to the enlargement of the lock chambers between Kingston and Montreal, so that the ships can be lengthened and widened without impairing their seaworthiness or appearance in any way.
Heretofore the boat-hull and cargo insurance rates have been sadly against the St. Lawrence route, causing double, and at times, three times as great a rate of insurance as those of New York and Boston, increasing materially by grounding in the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and Quebec, where ships were drawing a greater depth of water than there was in the river, or if loaded to the regulation deptli the fluctuation of water frequently causing them to ground, entailing heavy average and often more than average charges; or in other words, we hare been trying to force a 10,000 ton ship through a 5,000 ton channel. With the great draught of water, the channel being but three or four times the width of the ship, no room for action is left for the free movement of the ship, and grounding is the result. Here is the direct cause of the increased insurance rates, and at least it will be borne in mind that these extra rates of insurance have not only affected the ship but the cargo as well, both export and import, and in consequence import cargo has been diverted from the Canadian channel, finding its way through Boston and New York and over the Suspension bridge into Canada. The volume of this cargo, so diverted, will average 20,000 cars yearly, crossing the Niagara river for distribution in Hamilton, Toronto, London, Stratford and all western points. All through western Canada this will be overcome ; the rates of insurance will be cut in two, at least, for instead of the narrow contracted channel for deep draught ships, we have a river half a mile or more wide, where a ship drawing 18 or 19 feet can run full speed with impunity day or night, avoiding the grounding, tug bills, extra labour, and damage to the hull that the ocean ship is subject to.
In consequence of the frequent groundings in the St. Lawrence between Montreal and Quebec, the underwriters charged last year as high as $1.20 for every $100 of insurance and they figure on a loss in one case out of five.
During what period of time do they figure losing one vessel out of five ?

In one season, and that would be seen to lie the fact, judging by the high rate of insurance charges on the St. Lawrence route as compared with the Boston and New York routes.
Mr. MacLAREN <N. Perth).

That is absurd. They may charge on that basis, but it is not the fact.
ill-. MACLAREN (Perth). That may be, but we do not want to have to pay these high rates of insurance. I am not making any statement which I do not believe to be correct, and I think that I can prove pretty well any statements I make. Certainly a very large proportion of goods from the old country, intended for Canada, come via New York and Boston. I suppose that from 15,000 to 20,000 car loads annually come that way, across the Niagara river ; while nearly all these goods could be brought through the St. Lawrence route if we had our waterways properly equipped. It is a sad state of affairs to contemplate, that all this traffic has to come through foreign routes, when, by spending a little money, we could get it through our own St. Lawrence route.
The foregoing will give an idea of what my views are as to the method and manner of handling this class of freight. Now, there is another class of freight of the perishable nature, such as dairy produce, bacon and hams, and fruit and poultry, requiring faster transportation and cold storage. Special provision should be made as follows :
Ships of greater speed, at least 20 miles per hour, fitted for passenger trade, and being equipped with cold storage, should stop at leading points of shipment, or natural assembling points, or what may be termed express freight, such as butter, cheese, eggs, fruit, poultry, &c. These points should have two or three sailings each way each week. Each point above referred to would be supplied by the company with permanent cold storage facilities for the better protection of perishable freight. Warehouse receipts could be given to the dealer or producer, on which he could draw 50 to 75 per cent value of goods from the bank, and he could hold the goods in store until ready to ship, when he would get the best rail or steamship rate which could be procured. I feel safe in saying that the cost of transportation upon Canadian exports and imports would be very materially reduced by the inauguration of such a system. I also feel safe in saying that wheat from the North-west would be laid down at the seaboard, from Fort William' or Port Arthur, at from 5 cents to 6 cents a bushel, and a good profit made, a distance of 1,700 miles.
By this route the distance from Chicago, Duluth. Port Arthur and Fort William to Liverpool, would be almost 800 miles shorter than between the same points via New York.
The great difficulty I see is in getting our Canadian people to see and to grasp the great opportunities we have in store for us. I do not blame our railways for mak-

ing tlie best bargains with the people that they can, as business is business, and they are out for the profit. But I do blame our Canadian government and our Canadian people for sitting idly by, for not rising up and insisting that we should place our goods cn the markets of the world at as cheap a rate as our neighbours to the south of us. I heard an American gentleman state a few days ago that nature had provided us with seventeen hundred miles of the grandest waterway in the world, from the head of Lake Superior to the seaboard. He also said that if we could only assist nature a little in perfecting and developing our waterways, that we would in a very short time be in a position to place our goods on the market at as cheap a rate as they are doing it in the United States.
I will now, for argument's sake and comparison, give you a few quotations from an address which I delivered before the Dairymen's Association in Woodstock, in January of this year. In the first case I spoke of the export wheat trade from Buffalo to Liverpool. The rate of freight from Buffalo to Liverpool was lli cents per hundred liounds, while the rate from points in western Ontario to Liverpool was 21 cents per hundred pounds. Cattle from Toronto to Portland, 28 cents, cattle from Chicago to Portland, a distance of over 500 miles greater, 28 cents, cattle from Chicago to Montreal, 25 cents, cattle from the counties of Perth, Bruce, Huron or Grey, to Montreal, 33 cents to Montreal, or 8 cents more than from Chicago to Montreal. A car load of cattle from Listowel, a town in the county which I have the honour to represent, will cost $1.25 per head higher rate of freight than from Chicago to Montreal, a distance of over 400 miles longer haul than from Listowel.
_ In 1901 the United States shipped over 500,000 head of cattle to England. If they had paid at the same rate of freight we pay in Canada it would have cost them over $500,000 more. If they had paid for freight so much per mile it would have cost them $1,000,000 more.
The American jieople have developed 1,000 miles of their great waterway, starting, we might say, from Duluth, Chicago, Milwaukee, &c., to Buffalo. Twenty-two years ago, in 1880, the rail rate from Chicago to New York was 194 cents per bushel. In i899 the rail rate from Chicago to New York was 11 cents a bushel. During the same period by water the rate was as follows, between above named points :
1880	13 cents per bushel.
1899	 53	"	"
This steady decline in rates has been the direct result of waterway improvements at the Sault and other channels.
Now, another interesting feature about these rates, Mr. Speaker, is the cost. According to undisputed authority, the great
[ volume of tonnage which now passes through the Sault canal, and which this year exceeded 28,000,000 tons, was moved at a cost of 80-100ths of a mill per ton per mile. Tiie average cost upon trunk lines of railway in the United States is shown to be 8 mills per ton per mile, so we have here an object lesson that the United States waterway from Duluth and Chicago to Buffalo, 1,000 miles, is carrying freight for one-tenth the rate of the railways running parallel thereto. In other words, the waterway is doing for $1.00 wliat the railway would get $10 for.
It has been estimated by those identified with the commerce of the great lakes, that the 40,000,000 tons moved upon the lakes last year, west of Buffalo, if carried upon the basis of our railway rates, would have cost the American nation about $200,000.000 more than it did. and it is further estimated that at least 10,000,000 tons of the commerce passing through the Sault canals, would not have moved except for the facilities of water transportation. The railway charges upon it would have more than equalled its value at the point of destination. I have pointed out to the House the activity that is to be found upon the American waterways, its marvellous development and what a tremendous force it has been in the development of that country's western resources. Now, then, Mr. Speaker, I want the country to look for a moment at our own waterways, and what is the conspicuous feature ? That although wo have from the head of Lake Ontario to the seaboard a waterway unsurpassed, and to which we as a province have contributed about $47,000,000 for the improvement of the canals, &c., we have not a single vessel to carry our products to the seaboard. This is my answer and my solution for the condition that exists to-day in the country and the excessive railway tax that has been levied upon the people of our province-a province in which our agricultural interest represents an investment of $1,200,000,000, with an annual output of $300,000,000 of wealth wrung from its soil by the industry and labour of one and a quarter millions of our inhabitants.
If this great problem of transportation is solved upon true commercial lines we will quadruple our exports, we will double our farm Lands values, and besides utilizing our waterways in the summer time, we will more than double the freight to be handled by the railways. During the past year the rates of freight and insurance via our Montreal port have been so excessive as to be practically prohibitory. As an illustration- the rates from west of Toronto in Ontario have ruled about as follows to, say, London, England
Cheese, via Montreal, 88-90 cents per 100 pounds.
Cheese, via Portland, 55-50 per 100 pounds. Now, then, the House will observe that the

insurance rate is very high, via Montreal, it being from 40 cents per $100 to $1.20 per $100, while via Portland if was only 35 cents per $100. Why should the rate out of Montreal be 08 90 as against Portland 55 50? why should there be such a difference in the insurance? If we could reduce our freight rates in this country by utilizing our waterways as they do in the United States, the amount saved would buy a good many farms, a good many head of cattle and a good many boxes of cheese. Now, I simply give the House these few facts and figures which speak for themselves, and they are facts and figures which no one can dispute.
If the American people can utilize their waterways so as to make great reductions in their freight rate, why can we not do the same thing in this country? I, for one, think It could be done, and I would like to see the people of this country go right to work and do it. There is nothing in the world that we can do that will assist us in increasing the population of this country so much as that of reducing our freight rates. It is all right to talk about making more cheese and more butter, raising more cattle and hogs, more poultry, apples, eggs and dozens of other things which I might mention, but why should we go on in this way, spending so much time and money and doing so much hard work, when we can go to work and save so much money to the manufacturers and producers of our goods by spending a few million dollars, which will all come back to us in a few years and which will give us better rates of freight for the balance of our natural lives.

When you left the Chair at one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was speaking of the necessity of reducing freight rates on the various products of the farm, the field, the forest and the mine; and I was pointing out that a reduction in the freight rates would enable us, not only to make a greater profit, but to raise more butter, more cheese, more cattle, more poultry, more hogs, and so on and so on. I pointed out that our interest lay in utilizing our waterways so as to make great reductions in our freight rates. I may here say that after I concluded making the above remarks, or similar remarks, at the Woodstock Cheese Convention, Mr. Robert Ball-antyne, the chairman of the meeting, who is connected with one of the largest firms of exporters of cheese and butter in Canada and England, stood up and made the following remarks:
The facts an! figures presented by Mr. Mac-Laren are no doubt startling, and I know the rates are true, and I know the people of this district, west of Ontario, are more interested than the men of the east. I know you pay a much greater rate out of this section than the

men do out of the eastern section. I know the railway companies join together and agree among themselves to get a higher rate out of you by Montreal than they get out of you by Portland, and I know your cheeses are tremendously injured by shipping by Portland. I have had a lot of experience. I believe we were the biggest shippers out of Portland this last summer, and I believe we suffered enough to pay three rates out of Montreal. In quoting cheese to our customers -n England, if our quotation is sixpence higher, we cannot sell our cheese, and it is necessary to quote our cheese by the cheapest route in order to sell them. The facts of the matter are that the Canadian Pacific Railway use the St. Lawrence route and make that route by Quebec in order that they may make a competitive rate to get these goods by the Canadian Papins Railway and haul them to Quebec instead of Montreal. Mr. Speaker, I regret very much indeed that neither the govern-

ment nor the House had an opportunity of knowing about this amendment that has just been proposed by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. MacLaren). Hearing it read, as I have now for the first time, there does not seem to be anything very objectionable in the terms of the amendment, but under the circumstances I do not see how it is possible for the government to accept an amendment of this kind on a motion to go into Committee of Supply ; an amendment that we have not had an opportunity of reading or of considering before hand. I fear, therefore, that I will have to ask the House to vote against this amendment. As regards the speech which the hon. gentleman (Mr. MacLaren) lias delivered, I must say that I am very glad indeed to have the very valuable figures which he has placed before the House recorded in ' Hansard,' so that they may be thoroughly understood and known by hon. gentlemen and by the people of Canada. Many of these figures have already appeared in the public press, but not in such a form that they could be thoroughly understood and digested, and 1 must congratulate the hon. member upon the form in which he has put them before the House. The hon. gentleman, I am well aware, is deeply interested in all problems affecting agriculture, and especially the dairy trade of Canada, and I am quite sure that the results of his long study of these problems, as developed in the speech which has just been delivered, will be read by the members of the House and by the people of the country with a great deal of interest. My only regret is that the attendance of members was so scanty this morning, and that all who were here were not able to follow very closely my hon. friend's remarks. There are, however, one or two points which stand out particularly as the burden of his speech, to which I shall refer for a few moments.
One is that our waterways in Canada are defective and must be improved. Now, I venture to take issue with my hon. friend at once. The waterways of Canada are far superior to those of the United States. We have in the western lakes the same waterway opened to us as is opened to the United States. Whether the shipment starts from Duluth or from Fort William, that shipment can go down to the eastern end of Lake Brie just as well as to Port Colborne at the mouth of the Welland canal as it can to Buffalo, although the facilities at Port Colborne for handling the traffic are not as great as those at Buffalo. But that the government have already taken steps to remedy, and to-day there are large contracts being carried out for the improvement of Port Colborne, at the completion of which I venture to think that port will seriously rival the port of Buffalo in the facilities and advantages which it will afford for the transhipment of grain and other products
from the ships plying on the great lakes to those which ply on the canals.
My hon. friend has made a comparison between Buffalo and Montreal in regard to rates ; but I venture to think it is an unfair comparison, inasmuch as Montreal is a seaport, while Buffalo is separated by several hundred miles of either railway transport or very poor canar transport from tne American seaboard. Therefore the comparison between Buffalo and Montreal is an entirely unfair and unwarranted comparison.
My hon. friend has spoken about the American waterways having reduced the rates on American railroads. I have not studied this suuject in its entirety so as to be able to follow out that argument ; but from what I do know of railroad rates in the United States, I do not think the Erie canal from Buffalo to New York has materially affected them. If these rates are lower than the rates in Canada, it is due to two things : In the first place, the enormous traffic which has enabled them to grade their roaus better and to provide better accommodation ; and, secondly, the keen competition which exists between the large number of railroad corporations engaged in the carrying of goods from Chicago and other points in the west to the Atlantic seaboard.
It is true, there is a very serious discrimination against our agricultural products in Ontario, when we compare the cost of laying them down in England, the great market for our agricultural products, with the cost of laying down there American agricultural products, which come from points further west. This is one of the most grave difficulties which we have to overcome in connection with the export of our agricultural products to England ; and any proposition looking towards a solution of that difficulty is well worthy of the utmost consideration of parliament and the country. I venture to think that Canada has done in tne immeuiate past and is doing to-day a good deal to overcome that discrimination. In the first'place, within the last few years our canal system has been enlarged to a depin of 14 feet, so that now vessels carrying something uae 60,000 bushels of grain can leave the western end of the great lakes and carry their cargoes to Montreal without breaking bulk. This fact of itself makes our waterways far superior to the waterways of the United States, where no such cargo can be carried from the interior of the continent to the seaboard without breaking bulk at Buffalo and transhipping into smaller vessels to pass through the Erie canal. Notwithstanding this fact, the rates in Canada to the seaboard are a great deal higher tnan the rates in the United States for the same distance.
This difference in rates, is not. however, so much a difference in railroad rates on

this continent, as a difference in the rates on the Atlantic steamships.
This question is a serious one, with which this country lias been face to face for many years. It is one which the government nave been trying to deal with in what way they could. The fact which the hon. gentleman himself has brought forward, as to the insurance rates being so much higher on the St. Lawrence route than the insurance rates from Boston, New York and other American ports, is a very serious factor in this comparison of rates. That is a matter which has been before the government and the country for two or three years past ; and so important has it been felt to be by the government that if the hon. gentleman will look at the supplementary estimates which have been laid on the Table this morning for the year 1902-3, he will nud an item of $280,0(10 which is asked for by my hou. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the purpose of improving the lights and buoys auu ~*e otner aius to navigation on the river and gulf of St. Lawrence. These works, we believe, will have a material affect in reducing the rates of insurance on vessels using the St. Lawrence route. In fact, the insurance companies and the shipping companies have informed the government, that if the improvements involved in the scheme of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries are carried out, the result will be a reduction of the rates on the St. Lawrence route. My hon. friend will therefore see that not only are the government not unmindful of this question, but they have investigated it, and are prepared, if parliament grants this money, to go to work during the coming season and carry out me improvements which those familiar with the business have recommended to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
My hon. friend spoke about the discrimination in railroad rates. I do not know what can be done to remedy this discrimination except to appoint a railway commission. A Bill to create such a commission was introduced in the House this session and thoroughly discussed, and I hope that before the session closes it will be still further ventilated, so that the whole country will be fully seized with the subject. Next session I have no doubt that this measure will be re-introduced early enough to be carried into law, and it seems to me that a railway commission, such as is provided by this Bill, will be the simplest and most effective means of providing a remedy for the evils which now undoubtedly exist with regard to railway1 rates and transportation. At the moment I am not prepared to say to what extent the evils complained of interfere with our traffic. That is a question which will have to be settled by the railway commission. Individual instances will have to be submitted to that commission and evidence concerning them given under oath. And I am sure that no better
