tribunal than a commission of this kind, specially created for that work, could be devised to thoroughly sift the evils and disadvantages complained of and apply a remedy.
My hon. friend has also spoken about the necessity for encouraging a line of vessels to carry freight from the western end of our waterway down to Montreal. I regret extremely that such a line was not established long since, but the reason it has not been is no doubt the want of enterprise on the part of Canadians and their unwillingness to take every advantage of the waterways placed at their disposal by the country. We have a splendid chance of communication from Fort William to Montreal. Our coasting laws furnish every facility and encouragement for the establishment of lines of steamers on our great lakes, and if these facilities have not been taken advantage of, it seems to me that it is because the capitalists of this country have not seen their way clear to make the investment. I do not understand my hon. friend to suggest that the government should do any more than provide these facilities. It lias indeed been a matter of surprise to me that in days gone by a line of boats was not established to carry the enormous export trade of the Niagara peninsula, especially in fruit, from Hamilton and the adjoining ports down to Montreal. Instead of that, the railways have been allowed to monopolise that immense traffic. In view of the well established fact that water carriage is cheaper, especially in bulky freight, than rail carriage, I cannot understand why so small an amount of this western business has been carried in boats from the wrest to Montreal. That is one of the things that ought to be investigated. It is certainly astonishing that with the splendid facilities offered toy our canals and lakes there has not been any improvement in the direction of supplying vessels to carry this western trade.
I venture to say that in. addition there is abundant opportunity for me of enterprise to establish cold storage boats, which would run through Lake Erie and Ontario and down through the canals in summer to Montreal, where their freight would toe transhipped into ocean vessels, which are all equipped with cold storage facilities. I need not dwell on the facilities provided for cold storage freight from Montreal to Europe. My hon. friend himself read an extract which stoowed clearly that these are far superior to the advantages provided in American ports. His own cheese trade lias shown clearly that while the rates arc cheaper via Portland, the cheese becomes damaged on that route, whereas, although the rates may toe a little higher via Montreal, the cheese suffers no damage, hut arrives in good condition, and I think he will agree that it is better to pay a little higher freight at Montreal and have the cheese arrive in good order in our cold stor-

age vessels than ship It at a lower rate from American ports and have it arrive in a *damaged condition. I shall not say anything further on this point, except to remark that when my hon. friend asks us to help him in securing better accommodation at) Portland, he must not forget that Portland is a foreign port and that we have no control of the vessels leaving it.
My hon. friend is mistaken. I am not advocating any assistance to an American port, but simply that we should improve our Canadian waterways.

I understood my toon, friend to read and endorse the views expressed by a gentleman at the Dairymen's Association, who advised that we should provide better accommodation at Portland. I am not going into the figures which my hon. friend has given. They need to be studied very carefully before attempting to deal with them, but before sitting down, I would like to say to my hon. friend-and in so doing, I wish to set aside all politics, which he seemed to think ought to be introduced into the matter, since he brought his motion as an amendment to the resolution to go into supply. Such a motion, unless previously submitted to the government, is necessarily a motion of want of confidence.
I did give the Minister of Public Works a copy of the resolution yesterday.

My hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works was not here, and I did not know anything about it, nor did the other members of the government. But putting politics aside entirely, let me say that Canada as a whole, both this government and its predecessors, has devoted enormous sums of money to the solving of the transportation problem and has never shrunk from doing what the country thought necessary in order to provide transportation facilities. Our canal system is probably the greatest *on the face of the earth. Our government railway, the Intercolonial Railway, and the -Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway, both of which have been largely assisted by this country, are probably, in proportion to our wealth and population, the greatest railroad system on the globe. [DOT]Canada has borne, and is to-day bearing the burden, by paying the interest on the debt incurred for the purpose of perfecting our transportation facilities. These facilities are not at all utilized to their full extent. Our canal system is not utilized to the one-hundredth part of its capacity. If the enterprising capitalists of this country would undertake to supply the necessary vessels, there is nothing to prevent our canals being utilized in a way hitherto undreamed of, and i have no doubt that the investment
would prove profitable, both for the promoters and the country.
Under these circumstances, I venture to think that neither the government nor the people of Canada can be looked upon as recreant to this part of their duty or lacking in enterprise and determination to advance along the lines of material progress. If these facilities have not been utilized to the utmost possible extent, it is because the people of Canada have been devoting themselves to other things-the farmers to the production of goods, the merchants to selling those goods to advantage. And now they are beginning to see and understand that greater facilities in the way of transport are necessary, not in the shape of canals, not in the shape of railway tracks, but in the shape of improved rolling stock for the railways, and of ships for the utilization of the canals which now exist. The people of Canada will take that up and carry it out in a way commensurate with the facilities already at their disposal and commensurate with the enterprise they have shown in providing these facilities and in the development of the country's resources thus far. I am satisfied that hon. members on both sides and the people of Canada at large are expecting that this will be done, and I venture to think that, in the near future, such work will be done to greater advantage than heretofore. As I have said, I regret that it is impossible under the circumstances to accept the motion, especially in tiie form in which it has been given. But I sympathize with a great deal of wlfat has been said by the hon. member for North Perth, and I am satisfied that Canadians will take advantage of the facilities they have and will soon have a fleet upon our lakes that will rival that of the United States, and that will cause our trade to pass through our canals and ports instead of so much of it going to the south.

The motion now before the House is, perhaps, the most interesting for the farmers of this country that has yet been discussed. As the Minister of Railway's promises that next session he will introduce a Bill to regulate the traffic^ on the railways by establishing a railway commission, perhaps it will be well to wait and see what the government will do. The farmers are all deeply Interested in getting their products to the market at as cheap a rate as possible. It has been clearly established that Canadian farmers are discriminated against by the railways. Whether the commission will have power to relieve them of that discrimination remains to be seen. We find that to-day cattle are carried from Chicago to Boston at a cheaper rate than that which is charged on cattle from a point fifty miles north of Toronto to Boston over the same lines. I hold in my hands a shipping bill from Chicago for cattle shipped from there

for 28 cents per 100 pounds to Boston. X have another shipping bill from a point 80 miles north of Toronto for 33 cents per 100 pounds to Boston. And there is a rebate on the shipment from Chicago of $7.50, reducing the Chicago rate by about 3 cents further. Now, if this is a fact-and it is a fact, for I have the shipping bills here- it is a grievance whicli should be remedied.
1 have another shipping bill for cattle from Toronto to Boston for 25 cents per 100 pounds with no rebate. Now, this makes a difference of $1.14 on every beef weighing 1,400 pounds to get it on ship-board, the difference being against the Canadian farmers. I am credibly informed that, on the average, the American farmer has an advantage of $2 on every beef shipped to the ^ old country over the farmers of Canada. What does this mean ? It means that our farmers who are looking to better their condition will go and live in a land where they can get the best advantages. Is it any wonder that farm lands in Ontario and in Canada generally are depreciating in value when our railways discriminate against us in this way ? The Minister of Railways cannot establish his railway commission too soon. I am not prepared to condemn the government because they have not done it yet, for these discriminations have been going on for many years. But if the government will undertake to remedy this evil, the farmers will be satisfied. In the meantime, I am not prepared to condemn the government until we see what they are going to do in the matter.

I was a little surprised at the statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher), that this motion, being in amendment to a motion for Committee of Supply, must be regarded as a motion of want of confidence in the government. It is only a few days since the hon. gentleman's own friends accepted a motion in amendment to a motion for Committee of Supply from one of their own supporters, not regarding it as a motion of want of confidence. I refer to the motion of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) regarding the embargo on Canadian cattle. And the government could, with equal propriety, accept the motion now before the House, for there is nothing in it that goes any further or is any stronger than the motion offered by one of their own friends. The excuse that the Minister of Agriculture has given why this motion should not be allowed to pass, or his excuse for calling upon his friends to vote it down, is simply an excuse, and not a very good one either. The hon. minister said that the cold storage provided from Canadian ports is far superior to that provided from American ports. No doubt it is. Why, then, is it that the freight rates are so much higher from Canadian ports ? It must be due to one of two causes-either
Mr. ROBINSON West Elgin).
to want of competition in the vessels carrying on that trade or to the high insurance that is charged on the Canadian route. I have reason to believe that a good deal is due to the fact that the insurance on the St. Lawrence route is so very much higher than from American ports. And yet, strange to say, we have been told over and over again in this House, within the last few years by supporters of the government, that everything has been done that could be done to make the route as nearly perfect as possible-the lighting, deepening and enlarging of the channel and the affording of 14-foot navigation throughout the whole route. If everything has been done that should be done, why does the Minister of Agriculture tell us to-day that there is a large item in the supplementary estimates which have just been laid on the Table, for better lighting the St. Lawrence route ? I admit quite readily that the work is necessary. But the statement of the minister is strangely contradictory of what was said by Sir Louis Davies, the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries, over and over again in this House, that everything had been done that could be done to make the route perfect and to reduce the cost of insurance.
The Minister of Agriculture wonders that freight from the western part of Ontario is not carried in boats rather than in railways. Now the minister has been informing the Canadian farmer for several years past that he has introduced a system of cold storage on the railways, capable of carrying the perishable products of the farm to the seaboard, and laying them down in perfect condition; and he wonders because the farmers have taken him at his word and are availing themselves of this cold storage system. It is true that they have not found it as valuable as he declared it would be, but they have taken him at his word, and they are using it. Now I admit that if the Canadian farmer in the southwestern part of Ontario availed himself of steamers for the carriage of his fruit it might be to his advantage. But to do it successfully there would require to be better provision made for the carriage of that fruit on those steamers than exists at the present time. Why ? Because transportation is much slower, and there is a possibility of the fruit spoiling in the steamers as well as in the cars. But the Minister of Agriculture has made no provision for the better carriage of these perishable products of the farm by way of these steamers between, say, Hamilton or Grimsby and Montreal. Therefore it should not be a matter of surprise to the minister that they do not take advantage of the waterways; they cannot do so on account of the inferior transportation facilities that are afforded them by these steamers. The Minister of Agriculture says that the Canadians should take advantage of the splendid waterways provided by the country. Now, does it not occur to him that there

must be some defect, or otherwise they would take advantage of them? It may be in freight rates, it may be in the want of more rapid transportation, it may be in facilities for handling-there must be some reason why the people do not take advantage of it. The very fact that they do not take advantage of it ought to suggest to the hon. gentleman the necessity of inquiring into the cause and providing a remedy as early as possible. It is not enough to say that it is provided. These splendid waterways are not all they have been represented to be; the shippers of the country declare they are not what they have been represented to be. We often find Canadians shipping by way of American ports, availing themselves of the transportation facilities through American ports while leaving the waterways and railways of our own country. Then I say we cannot move one moment too soon in remedying these defects so that our shippers will take advantage of our waterways as they ought to be able to do.
The hon. minister told us a short time before that they had improved the St. Lawrence by lighting it better. Well, that is right, but they have contended for years that they have done all that was required; and the hon. gentleman's own friends have most positively assured us that everything was done that could be done. Only last session the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries stated that navigators found no fault with the St. Lawrence, that he had asked captains what more was necessary to be done, and they told him nothing, they could suggest nothing more to be done. But to-day the Minister of Agriculture tells us that there is an item of over $280,000 in the supplementary estimates presented to this House to-day for the purpose of better lighting the St. Lawrence route. There must have been something wrong, then. My impression is now, as it always has been, that the St. Lawrence was not as well lighted as it should be, otherwise the insurance rates would not be so high. It is evident there has been some defect in that route, and the minister now acknowledges it by making better provision for lighting it. The minister says the waterways of Canada are far superior to those of the United States. He said that in justification of the contention that we could ship cheaper to foreign markets through Canada than we could through the United States. The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. MacLaren) said that this justifies us in adopting his resolution, namely:
That in the opinion of this House it is both expedient and indispensable that the government should at once inaugurate such a policy in connection with our waterways and the shipbuilding industry of the country, as will speedily lead to the completion of the Canadian system by both inland and ocean transportation.
Now, the hon. minister says the waterways of Canada are far superior to the water-138
ways of the United States, and he gives that as an answer to the allegation that shipping is carried on more cheaply through the waterways of the United States than through those of Canada. Well, I know there is a good deal ini the fact that the larger country has a larger quantity to ship, that there is greater competition in vessels, and that perhaps the insurance is much fighter. Those facts may partly account for the larger quantity of shipping carried through the United States waterways. But I think there is another reason that accounts for it, and that is that we have not paid sufficient attention to our own waterways. There is no doubt of that whatever, in my judgment. I do not see any reason in the world why our railways cannot carry the produce of Canada, say from Windsor, if you like, to Montreal, as cheap as they can from Milwaukee, or St. Paul, or Minneapolis to Montreal. Why can they not do it ? Does it cost less or more to carry a hundred weight of freight fifteen hundred miles than it does to carry it a thousand miles ? It cost more to carry it a longer distance, and yet they are carrying it a longer distance for a cheaper price. What does that suggest ? Does it not suggest that there must be an overcharge on the freight carried through Canada? Does it not suggest the necessity of a railway commission, or some other power, to control the railways in fixing their freight rates ? It is not so much competiton that does that, because some railways carry freight through Canada and are taxed to their utmost capacity at times to handle it. Therefore they ought to be able to carry freight for Canadians at least as cheap, if not cheaper, than the Americans do, because sometimes they carry it a much longer distance.
Then there must be some other cause, and what is it ? The Canadians do not avail themselves of our splendid waterways. Why do they not ? There must be some shortage of vessels, and if there is a shortage of vessels, is not this resolution an appropriate one which suggests that the government should direct their attention to the matter :	' Inaugurate such a policy in connection with our waterways and the shipbuilding industry of the country as will speedily lead to the completion of the Canadian system toy both inland and ocean transportation.' Is that an improper suggestion to make to the government ? Is it improper for this House to ask the government to direct their attention to those things ?
We had a deputation here a few days ago waiting on the government asking them to give a bounty on ship-building. Suppose the government acceded to that request what would be the result ? It would certainly lead to the building of more ships in Canada and if we had more ships built in Canada there would be a better system of transportation. There would be a greater

43S7

competition and the result would be that we would have an ample supply of vessels for our carrying trade, whereas, we have not now an ample supply. We are many times short of what the country needs. This resolution could not be out of place if the government accepted it and there is no good reason in the world why the government should not accept it and say that we desire to do what is there proposed. We are directing our attention to the subject, but if we can get a spur, or any valuable suggestion from the opposition that will help us, we are willing and desirous to avail ourselves of such assistance and at the earliest possible moment to do everything we can to improve the shipping facilities of the country. We have been told that we have a 14 foot system of waterways from Lake Superior right down to Montreal. Some shippers say we have not. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) has told us over and over again that we have. But, whether we have or have not, we do And that vessel-owners are reluctant to avail themselves of our waterways to the extent that we would desire to see them do. There seems to be some reason for this and I say that it is the duty of the government to seek out that reason and remedy any defect that may be found to exist at the earliest possible moment. The hon. member who moved this resolution gave us some statistics to show the amount of trade that is passing through the Sault canal, the improvement in that trade and the value of it. The number of vessels that passed through the Sault canal last year was 2,041. Well, it suggested one thing to my mind and it was that there is ample competition in these waterways so far as our American friends are concerned and that if we had the same competition there is no doubt whatever but that it would result in the lowering of freight rates to the Canadian people. We find that a great deal of the grain that passes through the Sault canal is taken to Buffalo. We are told that it goes there because that is a cheaper route and some people say it is a cheaper route because they have better facilities for shipping to the seaboard. Their route does not compare with ours. The Brie canal is by no means equal to the St. Lawrence route. That does not affect the question, but the real reason is that they have better competition in railways from Buffalo to New York. I believe that fact accounts for the shipment of such a large amount of grain by this route rather than that the route from Buffalo to New York is superior to ours. It is by virtue of that competition that the freight rates are lower and that is the reason why a large portion of the grain is going that way rather than by way of Montreal. It is sometimes said that if we had the Georgian Bay canal this condition of affairs would be remedied. Well, it may be to some extent. I believe so far as the carriage

of the grain of the North-west Territories is concerned it would be of material advantage if we had it. The next question is whether the cost of that canal is not beyond the reach of the Canadian people at the present time, and whether we would be justified in incurring the very large expenditure which would be necessary to build that canal by the expected return from the shipping brought to the country on account of it. We do not think we would be at the present time, but we do think that the improvement of the other waterways should be proceeded with as rapidly as possible. We have heard it said over and over again in this House that since the present government came into power they have finished the St. Lawrence route, that our canal system is finished. We need only look at the estimates to satisfy ourselves that the canal system is not finished by any means, because we are spending money right along the same as we have done in years past. I do not complain of it, because I think that expenditure is absolutely necessary, but I think that the work might be hurried up a great deal faster than it has been carried on during the last four or five years. We have not made the progress we should have made. I think the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte)- with that constant discussion going on between three or four ministers of the Crown it is difficult to proceed. I desire to get their attention, because, if I can hope to make any impression upon them it will be through them hearing what I have to say. If they will only extend to me the courtesy of listening to ine I will be very much obliged. I have noticed this practice so often that I am obliged to speak of it. The hon. Minister of Public Works, in my judgment, has displayed more enterprise and energy in his efforts to carry this out than any other minister of the Crown, but I do say that during the last four or five years, although they said much about the expenditure and the work done by their predecessors, the work is going on more rapidly to-day than for many years past. This fact suggests to us the necessity of hurrying up, because as time goes on and new routes are being constructed it would be much more difficult to divert the trade of the country from these new routes when we get our own completed than to secure this trade if we had our routes ready for the carriage of the trade when the trade is offered to be carried. In going over the returns that were given to us a short time ago showing the quantity of grain going from ports on the Georgian Bay they show that a large share of that trade is being carried by railway notwithstanding all the money that we are spending on the waterways of this country. We have the Canada Atlantic Railway carrying millions and millions of bushels of grain from Parry Sound to Montreal, we have the Grand Trunk Railway carrying 11,000,-

000 or 12,000,000 bushels of grain from Midland every year to Montreal, and we have the Grand Trunk Railway carrying a large amount of wheat from Meaford, Colling-wood, Goderich and Sarnia to Montreal. All these railways are carrying the graiu and if facilities are given for the handling of the graiu at these ports through elevators and through improved facilities for transhipment it will materially assist in carrying the grain from these ports by these routes. The more grain that is carried in this way the less will be taken to Buffalo. If we continue to improve our waterways as we are doing by providing better lighting and reducing the cost of insurance and otherwise improving them we will induce the Canadian people to avail themselves of these routes, to ship their grain by Canadian routes rather than by American ro_utes as the hon. Minister of Agriculture told us they are doing. Our attention cannot be directed a moment too soon to the importance of this resolution and the hon. member for Perth is entitled to the thanks of this House as well as to the thanks of the shippers of the country and especially the agriculturists of the country for introducing this subject and giving the House the benefit of the large amount of information which he has collected in regard to it. The details which he has given to this House I rake to be approximately correct, as correct as it was possible for him to obtain them. It is valuable information, as I have said, and the introduction of the subject draws our attention to the subject in a way that should make the government desirous at the earliest possible date of directing their attention to it more energetically than they have done in the past. That being the case why should they not accept the resolution ? If the government have nothing to fear, if they have been doing all they could this would be a justification for what they have done. Then I say that the government should accept this resolution and let us pass it unanimously as they did in reference to the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) the other night in regard to the cattle trade of the country.

I have addressed the House so often on the transportation question, that I hesitate to speak once more; but the subject is off such vast importance that I may be pardoned; for saying a few words. My hon. friend (Mr. MacLaren) has rightly stated that it is perhaps the most important question that we have to deal with at the present time. The amalgamation of many lines of steamers on the Atlantic ocean has created a new interest in that question. No one can tell what the result of that may be, because it is too early yet to make any prophecy about it. There are those who believe that Mr. Morgan's plans are not only to amalgamate 138*
as many steamer lines as he can, but to work these lines in conjunction with the American railway system, and I am one of those who take that view. I believe that before we are very much older, we will find that Mr. Morgan and his syndicate who are stock holders in American railways will amalgamate both railways and steamship lines, not only on the ocean but on the lakes as well. In other words, they will be able to make a through rate from west to east There is no doubt that we are not in a position to-day to face such a strong combination, but I do not despair of the future of the country. We live in a century of progress and activity, and ships can be built in a very short time indeed. We are not so poor that we cannot provide for our needs in that direction. We have made a great deal of progress during the last year. I do not say that boastfully because I feel in my bones and sinews that this question is far above party politics. Our predecessors have worked in that direction more especially on the land, and the Canadian Pacific Railway was built and part of the canals completed. The completion of the Canadian Pacific Railway engaged our attention for several years, and not only our attention but our money and credit. Now we have to grapple with the problem of transportation as it is presented to us to-day. My hon. friend (Mr. MacLaren) should not lose sight of the progress we have made, and it is just as well that I should make it as clear as I can. We are improving our harbours on the lakes. The hon. gentleman has asked why our Canadian canal system has not developed more trade. The reason Is obvious. He has been to Buffalo and he has) seen the immense organization they have there, and that they have five miles of a breakwater in Buffalo harbour. On our side at Port Colborne, we had not a shadow of a harbour. How could a big ship loaded with grain or other produce come to Port Colborne when she iiad no accommodation there ? Well, we are equipping Port Colborne to-day and it will be so much done. Our system of canals is about completed, and the minister will have them lighted by electricity in order to make them more available. We are making improvements at Midland, Coliingwood, Owen Sound and Parry Sound, which are all reservoirs of trade. Let me call the attention of the House to the new policy of the Grand Trunk Railway. That company has been for a few years past an American road both in summer and winter, but I am glad to be able to say that Mr. Hays lias fully made up his mind to take advantage of the St. Lawrence route, and the Grand Trunk Railway is going to erect a large elevator and a large warehouse in the port of Montreal to accommodate their trade. This fact alone proves that we have made a great deal of progress, because if the St. Lawrence had not been improved the Grand Trunk Railway would not have come back

to Montreal. The route between Montreal and the sea is being improved as rapidly as money can improve it, and if my hou. friend (Mr. MacLaren, Perth) were in my position he could more readily appreciate the difficulty of carrying out such vast works. When I took office, for one reason or another, my department had no fleet of dredges. Dredges are not built in a day;
I had to organize the whole thing, and I regret that we are going to prorogue before the dredges are at work, because I had the intention of inviting the leaders of both sides of the House to make an inspection of the works on the St. Lawrence, but that will come another season. The port of Montreal is being equipped, and the port of Quebec will be equipped also. In spite of all the money we have spent in days past in Quebec, there is scarcely any space available for large vessels. The ships that carry freight from New York, Boston and Philadelphia take a whole world of merchandise on each voyage, and with the relatively inferior ships -which we had on our route in the past we could not compete with them.
speakername: The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. J. I. Tarte).

speechtext: Is it not a strange fact that the same ships sailing from Montreal and from Portland will carry freight from Portland at several shillings per hundred weight less than they will carry the same freight from Montreal.

There may be reasons for that, and one of the reasons is that most of the ships that sail from the American ports are larger than the average of those that in the past have been navigating our waters. W7e say in French : ' Paris n'a pas ete bati dans un jour '-Paris has not been built in a day-and energetic as we be, still a young nation like us cannot do everything in a day. I hope that before our hair is much grayer, we will have a fast line coupled with a line of freight carriers of the first magnitude, and then perhaps we will not be far from the solution of this difficult and expensive problem. We had to equip the St. Lawrence route in many ways. Our telegraph system to Belle Isle is completed; dredging is going on; the Minister of Marine is asking the House now for a sufficient sum of money to give a better service in lighting and buoying the river. Perhaps that should have been done sooner. At the same time, so far as the river between Quebec and Montreal is concerned, it might have been just as well to have waited a little, so that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries could have taken advantage of the new dredging work that has been going on in the channel. I do not believe that it is necessary to say more. My hon. friend from North Perth has, in a very particular way, called the attention of the House to that important question. The manner in which he has made his motion prevents our accepting it, because it ap-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
pears to be a motion of want of confidence.
I would not take it in that way, and I know he does not intend it as such; but I suppose the procedure of the House makes it necessai'y to so regard it. I think my hon. friend, after having given us the benefit of his experience and his ability in trade matters, can very well afford to withdraw his motion. It has been accepted in a friendly spirit. He has called the attention not only of the House, but of the commercial community to the necessity of going on as speedily as possible. Speaking for myself, I am very thankful to him for haying given us the great advantage of his knowledge and commercial ability in such matters.

Mr. Speaker, the importance of this subject to the western portion of this country is my only excuse for taking a few moments of the time of the House in discussing it. There is no issue before parliament of such great importance as the carrying trade, so far as the western portion of Canada is concerned. People are to-day going in there in thousands, and, as I had occasion to point out when the House first opened, the trade of that country was practically blocked during a great portion of the winter for the reason that we were not able to get the products of the country taken to the markets. The people are going in there in vast numbers, far in excess, I fear, of the enterprise of the government or any private enterprise to meet their future requirements. I may mention to the House a conversation which I had with the superintendent of the Canadian Pacific Railwmy when I waited upon him with regard to the shortage of cars. The burning question all over that country is how to get this great disability removed; and every person who has any influence at all is expected to exert it in that direction. I said to Mr. Leonard: ' Provided there are no more railroads opened up and we take nTorely the natural increase of acreage that will be broken up, and the natural increase of the produce that will come from the people now in the country, to say nothing of the people who are coming in, what are you going to do with the produce of that country six years from to-day ? ' His remark was : ' Mr. Boyd, ten railroads will not take the produce of this country out in double the time you at present seem to think it should.'
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is a question which this House might well consider, and it is this : The millers of Minneapolis, recognizing the importance of this great wheat field, have made an arrangement with the authorities at Washington, whereby they are permitted to grind wheat in Minneapolis in bond; and if our government and people do not rise to the emergency of the occasion, you may be prepared to see a great volume of the trade of that country pass-

ing to Minneapolis and other American cities. The point which my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works frequently refers to is the port of Buffalo. He speaks feelingly, and I believe sincerely, when he complains of the trade of this country passing from Buffalo to New York. But shippers have told me that the cheapness of the ocean carriage from New York to the European markets is the great cause of that. The immense shipping that goes into New York enables vessels to carry grain out at a much lower rate than it can be carried at from Montreal. A man told me that he lias actually had his grain carried free from Buffalo to New York, in order that it might be carried as ballast in vessels which were in a hurry to leave, when there was a great deal of shipping going on between New York and Liverpool. I fear that our Canadian ports will not be in a position to meet this competition until you are prepared to bonus vessels to come to .Montreal or to whatever winter port in Canada you may decide upon. This is a very important question, and the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. MacLaren) has done a good thing in again bringing it before the people; because I fear that a great many in eastern Canada do not recognize its urgent importance. I say it will require four railroads between Fort William and Winnipeg, and two or possibly three more cast of there to serve the trade that is looming up and is coming very soon in that country. It is only a short time since I went there, when we imported everything into the country-potatoes, meat, bread, everything ; whereas to-day the country is supplying all the demands of the people, feeding every person there, and at the same time has 100,000,000 bushels of grain for export, produced by a very small number of people. If you take out the towns and the cities, the number of people employed on the land in Manitoba and the North-west Territories is estimated, I think, by Sir William Van Horne, to be less than 40 per * cent of the population. Well, if 40 per cent of the present small population is able to produce such an enormous crop, what can we expect when that country has, as it must have in the near future, possibly 1,000,000 people ? What are you going to do to meet that emergency V It is only the importance of this question to the western country that induces me to occupy the time of the House at this moment. It is so important that the government should not lose sight of it, and the country will hold them responsible for whatever the results may be.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) made some reference to the Georgian Bay canal, in connection with the necessity of providing greater transportation facilities in the country. He said it was premature to c usider the question just now, because the
country was not prepared for it. But after j the House has listened to the sjjeech of the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd), who has given us his personal knowledge of the magnitude of the products of the country at the present time, and has referred to its still greater prospective products, I think every one will see the great necessity that exists for providing better facilities for carrying the products of the west to the seaboard.
The question of the Georgian Bay canal is one in which the people of the Ottawa valley are very much interested, and in which the people of the Dominion should likewise take a great interest, as it will no doubt be a great national waterway. There is no question but that the work is one of great necessity, and I am surprised and disappointed that the hon. Minister of Public Works has not a sum in the estimates for the construction of the French river route. I believed that he would have provided an amount for that purpose. I am disappointed also that he has not provided in the estimates for going on with the total survey, so that the country might have an idea of the probable cost. At all events, it is well understood that the cost will be in the neighbourhood of some $80,000,000, but that is a small item compared with the great advantages to be derived from the construction of this great undertaking. It is admitted to be the shortest route, and one on which freights may be transported with greater speed than on any existing route. I know that there is a sectional feeling in the west adverse to that enterprise, but it seems to me that we all ought to look at it in a national spirit. I know that some people are in favour of a company building that great work and others want the government to build it. For my part, I am in favour of the country doing the work, because I think that it will turn out a good asset. I believe that it will yield a good interest on the money expended. It would also be a great aid to colonization. Instead of the government employing immigrant agients in foreign countries to bring out immigrants, some of whom may be objectionable, their services could be dispensed with, as the construction of that work will attract a vast amount of labour, a considerable portion of which would settle, as they did when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, on places that are now regarded as unfit for settlement. It would not only help colonization, but develop the great water powers which we now have along the Ottawa river.
I am sorry that this subject was not taken up earlier in the session, and do not feel warranted in inflicting any lengthy remarks on the House at this period, but I do trust that the hon. Minister of Public Works, who is an active man, and who has given a part of this route at least his personal inspection, will go on vigorously with the

work next session, and obtain the consent of his colleagues to providing the necessary amount to start the French river route and then proceed with the whole undertaking.

I agree with the hon. gentleman who lias just taken his seat that it is very much to be regretted the discussion of this most important question did not take place at an earlier period, but in view of its vital importance to the Canadian consumer, I think that my hon. friend from North Perth was justified, even at this late hour, in drawing our attention to it. And in view of the very elaborate statement he has made and the amount of information he has given us regarding the discrimination in rates which prevail at present, he has, I consider, placed us under a great obligation to him.
I was glad to notice in the speech of the lion. Minister of Agriculture that he admitted there was nothing objectionable in the resolution as presented, and I regret that, under the circumstances, the government did not consent to its being accepted and passed unanimously. It is recognized on all hands that the question of transportation is the great national question in Canada to-day-one that ought not to be discussed from a party standpoint. The figures presented by my hon. friend are of such a character as to warrant our giving tile matter immediate attention, and the first place in our deliberations; and as my hon. friend gave notice yesterday to the lion. Minister of Public Works of his intention to propose this resolution, I do not think he has been treated with the courtesy which he was entitled to expect under the circumstances. It is hardly possible to take up a newspaper, no matter in wliat part of Canada it is published, and not find in its columns some reference to this transportation question. It is hardly possible not to find in any newspaper facts and figures showing the discrimination practised against the Canadian farmer and the advantages given the farmers of the United States to induce them to sliii) their products over Canadian routes to the sea. I cannot add anything to the facts and figures which have been presented by the hon. member for North Perth, but I have great pleasure in seconding the resolution, because I think the matter he has brought before the House is of vital interest to every consumer and' producer in this country.

As it is now so late in the session, and so much business has to be done before the adjournment, I do not propose to take up much of the time of the House in discussing this transportation question. It is a question whicli cannot be discussed in one day. I regret, in common with the hon. members who have spoken, that it was not brought up earlier in the session, but at the same time. I think Mr. MURRAY.
that my hon. friend from North Perth deserves to be commended for having drawn the attention of the House and the country, as he has done, to so many matters of interest. The facts and figures he has stated, we will now have on record, and will be of great advantage to us in future debates, in arriving at a solution of this problem. The transportation problem has many features, but there are three which seem to me of paramount importance. These are the equipping of the lower St. Lawrence in a suitable manner, the providing of suitable Canadian inland marine, and the adjusting of our inland freight charges. With regard to the St. Lawrence route, no doubt every lion, member is of the opinion that we must spare no pains or money to develop that waterway, and that in it are centred the' hopes of the country. We may differ as to the routes our products should take in the winter season, but during the open season of navigation it is in the interests of every province of the 1 )o-minion that the St. Lawrence route should be properly developed and equipped, so that vessels may use it under as favourable conditions as they do the competing American routes.
I would like to say a word about this question of marine insurance. If it were in the power of the government to tax vessels using the St. Lawrence route, say $5,000 each vessel oil each trip, I venture to think that the shipping people in Great Britain would carefully avoid it. Yet the same thing is done, if not by the government, by the insurance companies. The discrimination against that route by the insurance companies, as compared with American ports, amounts, on an ordinary freight carrier, to $25,000. It amounts to $5,000 per trip, and a fair estimate of the excess of insurance on a cargo of such a vessel would be, in a season, about $7,500. Therefore, there is a discrimination against every vessel trading in the St. Lawrence of from $30.000 to $35,000, as compared with vessels going to Boston, New York and Philadelphia.
We have heard that it is the intention of the government to spend $280,000 on further equipping the St. Lawrence route with whistles, buoys, lighthouses, signals and all that sort of thing. I would like to know if the government have ever consulted people who are thoroughly competent to judge of what it will cost to equip the St. Lawrence route so that vessels will be able to come in and trade on as good terms as are offered them in American ports. And, if the government have learned the facts, I would like very much to know what the cost will be.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WOmKS. My hon. friend the Minister of -Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Sutherland) before placin in the estimates the amount that is tuer

now, consulted parties wlio are most interested in Montreal and in the shipping trade ; and I feel confident that the amount In the estimates will be enough to light the St. Lawrence route in a very perfect way.

I am very glad to hear it. But, the point I want to make is this-that we, as members of this House of Commons should be convinced that we can make the St. Lawrence route so perfect that the rate of Insurance by that route can be made as low as that of any of the American ports. For my part, I am convinced that that can be accomplished. But I am not so sure, from the discussions I have heard in this House, that the members of the government have a policy before them by which they can actually accomplish that end. It seems to me that that cannot be accomplished by this expenditure of $280,000. But what 1 * wish is that we were convinced that we can make the St. Lawrence route as attractive to tramp vessels, In insurance rates and otherwise, as other routes. We have a number of British Canadian lines trading in the St. Lawrence, and we have captains who are accustomed to navigate that route. But I understand it is very difficult to get captains and officers who are accustomed to trade to other ports to come into the St. Lawrence. Therefore, this is a very much larger question, I think, than a great many have considered it to be. Until we can remove this discrimination on insurance rates in the St. Lawrence route, we cannot progress as we hope to do.
We have another handicap in this, that we have pilotage waters of three hundred miles. That handicap we cannot overcome but we can make the best arrangements possible.
It is not enough to talk of freight from Montreal or Quebec. It seems to me we are sending to those places as much as can be carried away with the facilities afforded. The next step, therefore, is .to see about the lower St. Lawrence and how we can induce ships to come in. I doubt that we will have to bonus the vessels to come into the route; it seems to me we can so improve the route that they will come in without that.
The question of the lack of a Canadian marine on the lakes has been discussed. I do not profess to offer a solution of that problem. Many views on that question have been expressed. It may be necessary, in the future, to protect these vessels in a way that . has never been done before; it may be necessary to bonus them. If the Americans have ships on the inland waters, we should have them too. Until we have Canadian bottoms on the lakes we cannot take advantage of the facilities afforded by our waterways. We do not need any new canals from Georgian bay to Montreal; we need to use those that we have. I would like very much to see made up by competent authority an estimate of the capacity of the St. Lawrence
canals-how many bushels of grain could be carried over them in a season ? I believe that if we had that information, we should see that we now have facilities for carrying all the grain that can be produced in Ontario and the North-west for many years to come.
Let me refer briefly to the question of freight charges. The hon. member for North Perth has placed this subject before the House in such a way that it will 'be very easy for us to get at the facts in the future. Some of these facts have come before the attention of hon. members from different sources in the past. In this case it is very difficult to know just what should be done. So far as the producers in this part of Canada are concerned, they are paying 20, 25 or 30 per cent more freight charges on their produce than their neighbours to the south are paying. Perhaps the difference is even greater in many cases. This will always be a grievance. So long as the people of Ontario permit to cross the line and see much more favourable conditions existing there, they will not be satisfied. It is for us to compare the conditions in the country to the south of us and in this country, and see whether we cannot place our finger upon the difficulty and furnish the remedy.
I shall not take up further time, I merely say, as I said in opening, that the hou. member for North Perth has done well, even at this late date of the session, in bringing the matter to the attention of the House, and I shall have much pleasure in supporting his resolution.

I regret very much that the hon. member for North Pertu did not reach this motion, which lie has had in contemplation for a long time, until so late a date that, it is impossible to deal with it in a satisfactory manner. However, I cannot let the opportunity pass without making a few remarks. The hon. gentleman dealt with a problem upon the wise solution of which depends the question whether Canada shall or shall not receive something like an adequate return for the money expended on the St. Lawrence canals. Two or three years ago, on looking into the question, I was surprised to find that, though Canada had gone on building and perfecting the St. Lawrence canals, so far as the returns of freight from Montreal showed, the amount of grain carried by that route was a diminishing quantity. Apparently, our whole outlay had been made upon a mistaken policy.

No, the reason, if my hon. friend will permit me to speak for a moment, is that, while we left Port Colborne unequipped, while we did not provide ourselves with proper railway facilities, our American friends were equipping Buffalo and equipping their railways in a way to make successful competi-

tion on our part difficult. That is the whole reason.

On looking into the matter further, I found the reason to be what has been pointed out in the brief remarks just made by the Hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte). In the first place the port of Montreal was not adequately equipped ; and in the second place the front door, as we may say, of the whole system, Port Colborne, was in such condition that no considerable volume of traffic could make its entrance to that route. Now, if we can, by any reasonable national expenditure, enable the people of Canada to receive from the St. Lawrence system of canals that return which I believe they can receive, the country will sustain the administration in making that expenditure. When the deepening of the canals to fourteen feet was spoken of and that result was looked forward to, and many persons interested in traffic in the lower provinces felt that the day was coming when a large inter-provincial trade would follow, when our heavy products, particularly coal and iron, would be carried in large quantities to the upper provinces, and we would receive in return, by cheap water carriage, an enormous quantity of food stuffs, manufactured goods and the imported articles of commerce from Quebec and Ontario. It has been stated to me by a person well qualified to judge that, if the St. Lawrence system were equipped with necessary facilities to use the extreme depth of fourteen feet, heavy freight, such as coal or iron ore, could be carried from the port of Pictou, or some other convenient port in Nova Scotia, to Port Arthur at the head of the lake system of navigation, at a cost not exceeding one dollar a ton. If that could be realized, it would mean an enormous market opening up for the coal mines of the lower provinces, a market which at present, those coal mines do not occupy ; for it is quite evident that, at present practically the whole coal supply of the province of Ontario and of the province of Quebec almost equally, comes from the United States.
We have in the lower provinces, particularly in the province of Nova Scotia, enormous supplies of coal which we are only too anxious to supply to our fellow citizens in the upper provinces from whom we buy so largely. The improvement of the business conducted over these canals would also have a great meaning for every prospective manufacturer of the lower provinces. One of those with which I have been connected was so handicapped, so hampered and embarrassed by the high cost of freight incurred in order to send the products of that business to the upper provinces where they found almost their entire market, that in the end they had to abandon the business as unprofitable. I am sure that nothing has been brought, before the House
this session, of so much importance as this great question of interprovineial traffic which has been opened up by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. MacLaren), and I am sorry that we have not the time to discuss it more fully. But I am glad to express my entire good-will towards any effort that may be made to improve that traffic; and I hope at a very early day to see realized a [DOT]system by which some of the ports in the lower provinces will ,be made shipping depots from which ocean steamers will go with great cargoes abroad, while these depots will be kept filled by a large fleet of river and lake carriers coming from the ports of the upper provinces, bringing grain and other products, and will then return to the west laden with our coal and other articles for which (we can find a market up above. There are so many considerations belonging to this matter that it is idle to attempt to touch them at this time, and I have only spoken in order to express the deep interest of my constituents in this question, and at the same time to express my warm approbation of the able and exhaustive manner in which this subject has been dealt with bv the hon. member for Perth.

At this late hour of tlie session, I do not intend to make any lengthy remarks. Still, I wish to mention one or two matters to the minister. In the first place, we all realize the great growth of the North-west, and are gratified at the enormous quantity of graiu that is being forwarded from that country. That is a reason for deepening the canals. But we want large vessels, large Canadian vessels, on the upper lakes ; and so long as it not definitely understood that the Minister of Public Works will not give to the Americans annually the right to use American vessels in bringing grain from one Canadian port to another Canadian port, I feel that the ship-building industry of Canada will not progress as it should.
That assurance has been given, and it has been carried out.
Now, wiill the country understand from this time forward that there never will be another privilege of that kind given by the government to carry grain from Port Arthur to Midland V

The Prime Minister has stated from his place in the House what our policy was. Now that policy in; the past lias been violated on one occasion, at the request of Mr. Booth, in order to allow him to carry grain from one Canadian port to another Canadian port.
If that policy can be relied on, I believe the ship-building industry will increase, and we will have Canadian vessels to carry our own grain.
There are ten new beats under construction now on the lakes.

If such is the case, I have no fear of Mr. Morgan and his syndicate ever absorbing Canadian vessels. There is in my opinion another cause that seriously interferes with grain going down the St. Lawrence. When grain reaches Port Colborne, it is there met with a tax of 15 cents a ton as a canal toll for passing through the Welland canal. Grain going to Buffalo goes through the Erie canal free. That 15 cents a ton is equal to about half a cent a bushel, or nearly so. In addition, as I mentioned in a previous session, the vessels have to lighten their cargo, if full loaded, and allow the railroad that lies along the Welland canal to' parry the, lighterage. If the government absorb that, so that a vessel could go from Duluth to Port Colborne with 100,000 bushels of grain, which she could take right through to Montreal, it would have a tendency to bring the grain through the St. Lawrence route, as the rates are often so high it does not pay to lighten. I have heard a great many vessel captains complain about the Welland canal tolls. They claim that the tolls on the grain are much larger than they are on iron ore or products of that kind. I' have been asked to draw the attention of the government to that fact. If they would remove those taxes, I believe it would have a great tendency to bring more grain through the canal. Then again at the port of Montreal 1 understand there are government taxes, while grain entering New York has to pay no charges of any kind.
The charges in New York are very much greater than they are in Montreal-charges of all kinds.
Well, when the grain arrives there, is there any government charge of any kind ?
The charges are higher than they are in Montreal.
I understood there were no government charges whatever in New York.
There are no government charges in Montreal, but there are harbour dues.

There are harbour dues in Montreal, but there are none In New York. That, they claim, interferes with the grain going through the St. Lawrence route. But the 15 cents a ton on grain passing through the Welland canal is a very serious affair. And when we take into consideration the insurance on the grain after it reaches Montreal, you will see that everything is against us. I have simply risen on this occasion to put before the government the request which I have
received from a number of vessel men to see if something cannot be done to remove these tolls, and thus place them on an equal footing with those who use the Erie canal. I am glad to support this resolution of the hon. member for Perth (Mr. MacLaren). I think it is well that he has brought it before the House, for I desire to see more grain carried through the St. Lawrence route than is now carried.
My hon friend from Perth will withdraw the motion, I hope.

I have no intention whatever of withdrawing the motion.
