speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, 1 wish to bring to the attention of the government and of the House u matter, which, though not so important as most of the subjects that hon. members from the west discuss, is still of very vital importance to the inhabitants of no less than four considerable towns in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. In the year 1882 an arrangement was made between the govern-l ment, represented by the Department of the Interior, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for speculation in four western towns. These were the towns of Yirden, Manitoba, Qu'Appelle, in Eastern Assiniboia, represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Douglas), Regina and Moosejaw in the district which I have the honour to represent. That arrangement was in the nature of a pool, the first part of the agreement being that each party, namely the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should contribute an equal portion of the lands necessary for these town sites. The arrangement is still in force. These four town sites were put into the hands of trustees to administer their affairs in the interests alike of the Canadian Pacific Railway and of the government. The government and the Canadian Pacific Railway were to participate equally in the net Proceeds. I may say that of all the policies which were adopted by the late Conservative *administration for the opening up of the Canadian North-west no single item or no part of the policy which that government adopted can be cited more appropriately than this as an illustration of the insanity- I think that the term is quite justifiable- which prevailed in the ideas of the hon. gentlemen who now occupy the opposition seats in this House in connection with what would be for the well being and progress
, Mr. MacLAREN (N Perth).

of that country. It seemed to be taken for granted at the inception of the opening up of the North-west Territories that that vast country was a vast preserve which might be made profitable to the private pockets of friends of the Conservative party. I think this particular matter of which I speak, illustrates as well as any other item of policy that notorious fact. I may mention, promising not to speak for any great length of time, some of the peculiar transactions of the trustees in whose hands the affairs of these town sites were placed. First, perhaps I had better state who the trustees were. These gentlemen were Mr. E. B. Angus, Sir Donald A. Smith, Mr. E. B. Osier, and Mr. W. B. Scarth. The affairs of these town sites are still in the hands of these gentlemen. They conducted business of various sorts. On some occasions they had transactions with the government, on other occasions they had transactions with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I may mention just a couple of instances which I may say were brought to light through the investigations made by a commission which was appointed two years ago by the government to inquire into the affairs of these town sites. I mention these instances to show the character of the transactions which the trustees thought proper to enter into. In one case they sold part of a town site to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Some time subsequent to the year 1897 the trustees sold part of the town site of Moosejaw to the Canadian Pacific Railway, 33 acres in extent, at the price of $3 per acre. When the commissioners who were appointed two years ago to make an investigation into the affairs of these town sites, took evidence at Moosejaw they received the evidence of the trustees' own agent in the town to the effect that this land which had been sold to the Canadian Pacific Railway for $3 per acre, was in reality worth 850 per acre. This was evidence tendered by the agent of the trustees. There was also a transaction in Regina in connection with a building. In the early days the trustees erected a brick veneered building in Regina at a cost of $15,000. They rented that building for a number of years to the government, and in all the government paid them a rental of $17,435. Later still the trustees sold the building to the government and the government paid them $16,000, so that in all the trustees received from the government $33,435 for the building whose first cost in the early days, at a time when building was very expensive in that country, was only SlsjoOO. The House will at once recognize that there was a material difference in the nature of the business transacted with the Canadian Pacific Railway and the business transacted with the government. Another most peculiar item of their business which was brought to light by the investigation of the commissioners was in connection with the town site of Virden. The arrangement [DOT] made between the government and the company was that an equal portion of land for each town site should be contributed by each. When the town site of Virden was located, there was a gentleman named Mr. T. M. Daly who entered for half a section of the land. Mr. Daly, as probably the House is well aware, was a very prominent member of the Conservative party, and he was later on Minister of the Interior in the Conservative government. Another quarter section of the land which afterwards formed that town site had been entered for by a lady named Mrs. Willis. The government cancelled the entry of Mrs. Willis, and thereby came into possession of her quarter section. The government also was the possessor of the fourth quarter section, and the other two quarter sections had been entered for by Mr. Daly. Mr. Daly had not commenced his homestead duties, and the records of the department show that he voluntarily abandoned his entry, but when the commissioners, two years ago made their investigation, they found that an amount of $6,400 had been paid to Mr. Daly on account of this half section of land entered for by him, but which he had subsequently abandoned as far as the records in the Interior Department disclose. A further fact disclosed was, that, notwithstanding that the government had contributed the other half of the town site, the quarter section that had been entered for by Mrs. Willis, which had been cancelled, and the quarter section which the government always owned, they were charged in the books of the town site trustees with half of this $6,400 which had been paid to Mr. Daly.
In what year was the entry made by Mr. Daly ?

I will give that information later. I do not bring up this matter for the purpose of entering into any personal or political recriminations, but to urge that the people of these four towns have laboured under a very serious handicap for years on account of this town site arrangement, by reason of an exemption from taxation enjoyed by the .trustees. The government hold one-half interest and the Canadian Pacific Railway. Company held only in reality a quarter interest. It will be necessary for me to explain that before the arrangement was actually made between the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had made a prior arrangement with a company called the North-west Land Company, and this latter company was brought in and made a party in this town site arrangement. Since 1882, when these town sites were constituted, the position has been that the government owned one-half interest in the net proceeds of these town sites, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company having one-quarter interest, and the North-west Land Company the other quarter interest. The interest of the govern' ment was exempt from taxation, and

under tlie terms of the Canadian Pacific Railway contract of 1881, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company contended that their quarter interest was also exempt from taxation. I do not think the matter went so far as a law suit, but after considerable negotiations, an arrangement was made- and the municipalities were led to believe that they were compelled to agree to the arrangement-by which only one-quarter of the taxes should be collected by the municipalities from the trustees. For nearly twenty years, on a considerable portion of each of these four town sites, the municipalities have been able to collect only oue-quarter of the amount of taxes which should properly have beeu paid. This is the phase of the question which I have risen chiefly to bring to the attention of the government and of the House. In the year 1891 the right hou. leader of the government visited the North-west, and this town site matter was brought to his attention, and speaking at Moosejaw upon his responsibility as the leader of a great party in this country, he said :
In his opinion it was an improper thing for the government to be holding property in this way for speculative purposes to the detriment of municipalities.
The right hon. gentleman has now been leader of the government of Canada since 1890, and the people of these towns are thinking that it is time that the pledge which in effect he gave in the town of Moosejaw in 1894, should be implemented by action. I may state that for a considerable length of time past efforts have been made by the Minister of the Interior in the direction, as we have understood it, of relieving these municipalities from the handicap which they labour under, and I believe it was the efforts which the minister was making which led to the appointment of this commission two years ago to inquire into the affairs of the town sites trust, because certain difficulties had been encountered in the way of giving the relief which is necessary. I am given to understand that within recent weeks an arrangement has been practically entered into by the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for the division of the property of these town sites, by which an equal division shall be made in each town, the Canadian Pacific Railway accepting one-half and the government assuming control and possession of the other half. I am very glad to know that the arrangement is likely to he very shortly completed, but wbat I want to do this afternoon is to urge upon the government to, at the earliest possible moment, dispossess themselves of this property so that the property may become liable to the ordinary taxation. I go further, and I urge that it would be only fair and reasonable, in place of putting the property up at auction and thereby tending to some extent to depreciate, for the time being at Mr. SCOTT.
least, the value of this property itself and of all the other property in these towns; it would be only fair and reasonable for the government to hand over to these municipalities the half portion which comes to the government in. the division. As a reason for this request, I would point out that the total receipts of the trustees from these town sites up to the present time have been: in the case of Regina, $254,485.92, and in the case of Moosejaw, $114,006.63. These amounts were the net proceeds to the trustees from two of the four towns. The government have received from these four town sites no less sum a than $141,200. There is still due to the government from the trustees-or at least there was when the commissioners made their report, and so far as I know this amount has not been, paid since, although it may have been paid without my knowledge-there was still due to the government when the commissioners made their report a sum of $46,855.99. This was some $30,000 more than was to the credit of the government on the trustees books, but the commissioners found that some of the bookkeeping of the trustees was very peculiar, and they stated in their report that there should be paid to the government by the trustees about $30,000 more than was credited to tbe government on the books. In view of the fact that these municipalities have been handicapped and have been losing very considerable amounts through the peculiar position iu which a great part of the property within them was placed.
I think it is only fair that their request be granted now, and that the government's portion of these town sites should be handed over to the municipalities. In the case of Regina, the amount of taxes which should have been paid by the trustees in these years is $56,054.60. The amount of taxes which was actually paid is only $14,013.65, leaving a loss to the town of $42,040.95. It is therefore only reasonable and fair tliat tbe government should put these municipalities in the possession of this property, rather than to throw the whole property on the market by auction sale. But, however, the property may be disposed of, I would urge most strongly on the government and on the House the rightfulness of the government becoming dispossessed of their property in these towns at the earliest possible moment, so that the handicap against the towns which for nearly twenty years has prevailed, shall be removed at last.

Mr. Speaker, personally I have no thought one way or the other whether it would be better for the government to transfer these town sites to the municipalities or to keep them; but I must deal very shortly with some of the remarks made by the hon. member. When this question was brought up in the House two or three years ago, I thought I answered the accusation which was made *

against the trustees as fairly and squarely as any man could expect who asked for an explanation. I stated at that time, and I state again, that the report which the commissioners brought in was a partisan report, got up for a particular purpose, a report which the trustees absolutely contradicted; and I am rather surprised that any one should get up in this House and by implication say that Lord Strathcona, Mr. Angus, Mr. Scarth and myself had rendered false returns to the government, had cooked accounts and had been guilty of doubtful book-keeping. I do not think that statement requires a contradiction from me in this House or anywhere. With regard to these town sites or the administration of them, I make the statement that there has never been a fund in Canada administered as well, as faithfully, as honestly, in the interest of the trust and for the benefit of the country. Charges were made as to the proper distribution of certain accounts, as to the power of the trustees to expend money for building purposes, and to allot a part of the land for railway purposes or for government purposes. In that connection- I am speaking from memory, not having the figures before me-the government received in the proportion of two to one in round figures as against the railway company. The trustees acted entirely within the rights of the trust, and no action was done by the trustees except under the conditions imposed by the trust. They were empowered to expend money for the development and for the benefit of the towns. For many years past the trustees have endeavoured to get themselves freed from further participation in the matter; but the government put every check and obstacle in their way to prevent a division of these town sites. When the report of the commission, which I say was an absolutely partisan report, was brought in, making the claim that the trustees were debtors to the government to the amount of $30,COO or $40,000, because of certain expenditures they had made under the trust, the trustees at once demanded that the government should take action against them in court to recover that money. The trustees from that day to this have endeavoured to have that matter brought to an issue, but have not been able to do so, and an hon. member from the North-west now accuses these gentlemen of having mal-administered the trust, although the government have refused to bring an action, and there is no possible means by which the trustees can shake themselves free of the matter, so as to be in a position to show that the report of this commission was false and partisan, and was got up for a special purpose. That commission expected to find maladministration, but they were unable to find any; and the government have failed to bring the question to an issue. The trustees of that fund handled property to the extent, if my recollection serves me rightly, of between one million and one
million and a half dollars; and during the time of the sales no member of that trust, so far as I recollect, had anything to do with the government. I was not at that time a member of parliament; I was simply a private individual acting as a trustee. From the inception of the trust to this day no trustee has been paid a single dollar of commission, nor one dollar for travelling expenses or as fees for attending meetings or for any other purpose, with the exception, as I think I explained to the House two years ago, that I drew $250 or $500 for the purpose of giving bonuses to some of the clerks in the office of the trustees when they were dismissed or when the office was removed from Toronto to Winnipeg. I do not mind having these things ventilated in court if a charge is laid or a claim is made; but I do certainly object to a member getting up in this House and making statements which leave the impression on the House, whether intentionally or not, that there was wrong-doing on the part of the trustees. I say that the government, either wilfully or through absolute neglect, have refused to bring the matter to an issue in court. Each of the four trustees has done his best, both by himself and through his solicitors, to get the matter brought to an issue. I do not wish to speak any further on the subject, but I do object to statements of this sort being made in the House when the conditions should be thoroughly known, and I think it is entirely improper that any member of this House should make accusations reflecting upon the character of Lord Strathcona and Mr. It. B. Angus, when they are not here to answer for themselves. For myself, I am ready to answer anything.

The question as to whether the trustees did or did not improperly charge any money to the government is a question that cannot be settled by statements on the floor of this House, but has to be settled in the ordinary way through the courts; and the department have taken steps to have it settled in that way. The department found some time ago that it was necessary to have an investigation of the accounts of this trust, aid a comiu ssion was issued 'or that purpose. Tno commission consisted of E. F. Steplr n-son, inspector of Dominion lands agents, and Mr. Smart, the Deputy Minister of the Interior. They made a report, as has been stated by my hon. friend from West Assi-niboia (Mr. Scott). The report showed that, in the opinion of the commissioners, a considerable sum. I think about $30,000, had been improperly charged to the government. The trustees disputed this finding of the commission. The action taken by the department has been this : Pending the settlement of the dispute, as to this alleged improper charge, we have entered into an agreement with the Canadian Pacific Rail-

way Company and the Canada North-west Land Company, by which the town lots which are still unsold have been divided. Within the past few weeks the Land Commissioner of the government and an officer of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, acting for the other party, have made a division of the lots, and there only remains to be settled the question as to the final closing of the accounts between the trustees and the government. The Department of Justice has been instructed to take action for the purpose of having this matter settled in court. 1 presume that the action is now pending. As to the difficulties under which the corporations have laboured, 1 sympathize with the view of my hon. friend at least to this extent, that I do not think the towns should be left with such a considerable portion of their area not liable to taxation; and I have intimated to him that steps will be taken to bring the government's interest in the town sites to an end. Whether that will be done by disposing of the lots by auction or otherwise 1 am not in a position to say; but I think the government should not hold simply for speculative purposes a considerable area of a town, as it imposes an undue and unfair burden on the town population. My hon. friend has urged very strongly that this amount ought to be contributed by the government to the town corporation as a free gift in return for the exemption from taxes during the past year. I have not been able to give an affirmative answer to that proposition, and I cannot say what decision the government will arrive at, but the question will be taken up and disposed of iu a very short time. The division of the town lots between the commissioner of the company and the commissioner of the government, has only taken place within the last few weeks, and at this period of the session we are unable to deal with it; but as soon as the'session is over, and I have sufficient time to look into the matter, the whole transaction will be closed up.

beg to move :

Motion agreed to, and House went into committee thereon.
What is the object of this 7

I might say that if we were not renewing a charter I would not vote for the Bill. I feel that in granting charters we should be very careful indeed, especially when we have to deal with our rivers and waterways. The French river and Lake Nipissing can no more be called a canal than I may bo called the Pope or the King of England. The French river is essentially a navigable river, a deep waterway. Again, if parliament had not granted a charter to people

who have advertised that great waterway,
I would not feel inclined to-day to grant this charter, but as parliament many years ago has granted the charter and as there are, t'o a certain extent, vested rights, I think it is only fair that the charter should be renewed. On the other hand, the promoters themselves recognize and admit that the French river is not in the same position at all as the other parts covered by the charter. The Mattawa and Ottawa rivers must be canalized in certain parts if we want to have a waterway twenty feet deep to the St. Lawrence. I would not undertake to say that that depth of water can be easily got from Lake Nipissing down to the city of Montreal. I have not the necessary inforihation to form a correct opinion; my department has no survey of the Mattawa and of the Ottawa rivers. I have, however, a complete and careful survey of the French river. I have plans prepared, and if parliament made up its mind to grant a contract there would be very little to be done before having tenders called for. I repeat that the French river is essentially a navigable river, and that is the reason why I have asked the promoters of the Bill to consent to the amendment or addition which I have just suggested. I feel that this country must keep the control of that waterway. Of course, nothing can be done by any department of state without the consent of parliament. This clause that I am suggesting does not pledge us to anything; it gives us only more freedom. If the Governor General in Council later on believes that the company which is seeking for the renewal of their charter offers sufficient guarantees to go on with the whole work, an Order in Council will decide. If not, well, we might later on come to the House and ask for the amount necessary to improve the French river so as to make it a waterway twenty feet deep. I will not discuss the features of that work to-night, because we have discussed it already on many occasions, and I believe this would not be the time to offer any lengthy discussion of it. Before I take my seat, let me thank those who have done the very useful work of calling puSlic attention to that magnificent waterway. I confess that I did not know anything about it before I read all the prospectuses, all the articles and pamphlets published by the Georgian Bay Canal Company. They deserve consideration at our hands, great consideration at our hands, and that is the main reason why I made up my mind-speaking for myself-to consent to the renewal of their charter. It is said that the company can find the money necessary to carry out the work they have in hand, namely, to canalize and improve the Mattawa and the Ottawa rivers, without asking any grant of public money. I hope it is the case. I am not sure about it though, but I hope it is the case. If it is the case, and if we are not called upon I
to give them any guarantee or any subsidy, well, I suppose, we can afford to let them go on with the work.

If this waterway is ever improved, so as to make it one of the great highways of commerce and to become a competing line with the other highways both in our own and the neighbouring country, it can only be successfully accomplished by having no toll gates on the route. The fact that tolls are contemplated is, to my mind, one of the very strongest objections to allowing any private company to take over that waterway and build the canal. There is no doubt that if it ever becomes half as useful as the promoters of this Bill tell the public it will become, it is desirable that the government should build it. The probability of a company building it without any guarantee or bonus or assistance from the government seems to me to be extremely problematical. So far as it goes, I think this amendment is in the right direction, namely, to hold under the control of the government at least a portion of the route, and it would be much more agreeable to my views if they held the whole of it. I confess that there is a great deal in what the Minister of Public Works has said. This company has, in a measure, some'"fesfed rights, because they have been working at it for a long time, and they have spent a good deal of money on it. However, I do not think that even that should be a justification for a private company holding any one of the great waterways of commerce.'

Let my hon. friend remember that if these gentlemen go on with the work, it will be always our right to take possession of the work by only paying the amount that will have been actually spent; so there is no great danger after all.
But we know how these accounts are usually made up when the government comes to take them over.
There is no immediate danger, I think.

As being in charge of the Bill I wish to say that the gentlemen who asked me to place the Bill before the House have instructed me to consent to the amendment proposed by the Minister of Public Works. In doing so, I wish to say that I have heard with considerable satisfaction the opinions expressed by the Minister of Public Works. I cannot help indulging in a little self-congratulation in the matter. I look back four years to the time when our good friend, Mr. Poupore, who so ably represented the county of Pontiac and myself brought this subject to the attention of the House. But it is not so much for the purpose of congratulating Mr. Poupore and myself that I rise, as to express the great satisfaction and pleasure that I feel in seeing the progress which this project

has made since 1898. I am delighted to see that those who have charge of the affairs of this country have realized the tremendous, I. might almost say the vital importance and necessity of this great highway. The tremendous development which has taken place in the North-west and Canada generally has made that route an absolute necessity and one which in importance, I think, does not take second place even to the Can adian Pacific Railway-
Oh, oh.

I know that my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) does not agree with me, but I think the time is not far distant when that hon. gentleman himself will aceept that view. I hope the government will take the matter into very serious contemplation ; and, if they are not prepared to allow this company to go on and build the canal, they will themselves, at an early day, enter upon the construction of it.

I am sorry that I came in too late to hear the first part of this discussion. X understand that the object of this Bill is to give a private corporation power to make a waterway from the French river to Montreal. While I am in favour of developing our canal system and of spending public money in carrying out public works, I am opposed to granting to a private company the right of control over waterways. We have before us great problems, but none I think greater than the problem of providing means of transport for the increasing produce of the west to the seaboard. We are spending enormous sums of money-from my point of view we are throwing away enormous sums on useless works-but, while I do not approve of some of the expenditures that are being made, I do believe that the government ought to develop to the fullest extent our transportation system. If the Georgian Bay canal can be made part of our waterway system, if with any reasonable expenditure of money it can be made iso successful that by it the grain of the North-west can be carried to the seaboard more cheaply than by rail or by the present waterways, I am in favour of it being made a national work. So far as I know, there is not before the country to-day information showing what that undertaking will cost.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) will allow me, I would like to say that I am in a position to state that the improvement of the French river so as to make it a twenty-foot ship waterway from Georgian Bay to Lake Ni-pissing would not cost more than $5,000,000, and I would expect to carry it out for less. I have accurate plans of the whole work.
And how about the other end of the work ?	.
I do not know about that.
Would that $5,000,000 complete the route to North Bay ?
North Bay is on Lake Nipissing. Yes, that would build it to North Bay or to some other point on Lake Nipissing.

As I say, I was not here at the opening of this discussion. But I understood that this was a Bill covering the whole system from Georgian Bay to the St. Lawrence at or near Montreal, and that it is proposed to hand over the control of that waterway to a company. I am against any private company controlling that waterway or any part of it. If it is to be a waterway developed in the interest of Canada the government should control it. Possibly it is an undertaking that the country should assume, but I believe we have not before us official records of the cost. '
Yes we have.
We have records of long ago.
No, last year.

But what I wish to say and I say it without reserve, is that the waterways of the country should not be allowed to pass into private hands. Let the railways be privately owned if you like. Railways can be built by anybody. But it js not so with waterways, they are nature's courses through the country. You can duplicate a railway but-
We will bring this canal around by Toronto and then it will be all right.

I think it is a great compliment to my hon. friends from Toronto and myself that whenever we propose anything in the public interest we are taunted with being moved by consideration for the interests of Toronto. I deny that I represent the interests of Toronto alone or that my views are influenced by any consideration but that of the public interest.
Oh, oh.
Canadian Pacific Railway.

I deny that I have ever voted or spoken in the interest of the Canadian Pacific Railway in this House. I am astonished that members of this House, and even ministers of the Crown, lacking any other answer to what I have said at different times, should so often reply with the taunt :	Oh, you speak as you do because
you belong to the Canadian Pacific Railway company. It shows but a poor conception of their position and duties as members of this House that they cannot conceive of a

man taking an independent position on tliis floor, that they cannot conceive of a member of this House sinking his individual interest in the interest of the country. 1 deny for my part, that I am not able to sink my own interests if they conflict with the ih-terests of the country. And I defy any member of this House to point to a speech or vote, or canvass of mine-I have never canvassed a member of this House for any vote-that was in the interests of any corporation or any section. It is my right to object to this Bill or any other that comes up in this House. If I make arguments that are not convincing that is my fault or it is due to the weakness of my case. But I have the right to my opinion and the right to state it without being taunted with speaking in the interests of any corporation. The members of this House, I think unanimously recognize that the transportation question is the one question before us in Canada to-day. My colleagues from Toronto and I are taunted with selfishness and with consideration only for Toronto's interests. Has there been a voice raised from any member from Toronto against the expenditure of money in Montreal harbour or the Quebec harbour, or for the purpose of deepening the St. Lawrence channel ? Every member from the west has held up both hands for the development of a seaport. X agree that the most important question before the House and the people to-day is the transportation question. So far as the west and local conditions in the west are concerned that problem will take care of itself. But, as we near the seaboard, the government must take that harbour in hand. When we reach Montreal or Quebec, or whatever port it may be, the government must take charge of this problem.
No proposition to increase the transportation facilities on the St. Lawrence will be voted down by any member from the west. But what I say in connection with this Bill and 1 feel it sincerely, is that no public waterway in this country should be allowed to fall into the hands of a private corporation. This waterway that is now under discussion is more than a mere waterway, it means control of perhaps the greatest electric power that we have on this continent. The private corporation who obtains control of the canal, controls by virtue of that charter the water power all along that route. Now, in view of the development of electrical power and the possibilities that are before us, who can say what that power will be worth in ten years ? The cheapness of production is dependent altogether upon the cheapness of our water power. If that water power gets into the hands of private individuals they will control the cost of production in this country, and they will control the transportation problem.
I do not think that any member of the government, any member on that side of the House, will say that our waterway trans- 1 139
portation is satisfactory to-day. It is very unsatisfactory. We complain of want of shipping ; we complain of want of proper transportation facilities. I can tell this House that there is capital in abundance and to spare to build every vessel 'that Is wanted to take control of Canadian shipping. Men are ready and willing to put their money into this business, and all that is wanted is a proper channel to transport our grain, the production of which is sure to increase enormously from year to year. Our grain production will shortly be such as we have at present no conception of. Let me give an illustration. I have a letter from a gentleman from Scotland who was in the capital a few weeks ago. He went to the North-west and travelled over the Calgary and Edmonton Railway. He writes a letter to his board of directors in Great Britain, of which he sent me a copy, and in which he says that from Calgary north to Edmonton, for thirty miles on each side of that road, there is more good agricultural land than there is in all Scotland. Now when you have a small stretch of country of which that can be said, what is going to be the production of that country in ten years ? What strikes me in this House is that when important Bills like this are before us, as a rule we regard them from the point of view of to-day, we are not looking forward five years, much less ten years. We are granting charters giving control of our public waterways, in this case canal privileges the importance of which not one member of the House realizes, handing over to this company this enormous privilege, equivalent to a tax of perhaps many cents a bushel on all the grain that is grown in the North-west for twenty years. Twenty years is a very short time in the life of a nation, a nation as we are just beginning to develop our resources. I for one, Mr. Chairman, will oppose to the best of my ability the granting of charters such as tliis, giving into private hands the control of what must be eventually an enormously valuable public franchise.

I share to a large extent the views just expressed by my hon. friend. I have stated those views on several occasions, here and elsewhere. I have said we should not hand over our waterways and our rivers to any private corporation. This vast Dominion is wide, and there is plenty of land for railways. But there are not many Ottawa rivers, there are not many French rivers. The facts of this case have to be taken into consideration. In 1894 parliament granted a charter to the Georgian Bay Canal Company, which charter was renewed in 1898. One of the clauses of the charter granted in 1894 reads as follows :
Her Majesty, her heirs and sale lessors, may at any time assume the possession and property of the said canals and works, and ot all the



rights and privileges and advantages of the Company, all of which shall after such assumption be vested in Her Majesty, her heirs and successors, on giving to the company one week's notice thereof and on paying lo the company the value of the same, to be fixed by three arbitrators, or the majority of them, "re to be chosen by the government, another by the company and a third arbitrator by the two arbitrators.
Now, if I had not found this clause In that charter 1 would not for a moment have consented to any renewal of the charter. But this clause being here, the charter having been renewed twice, the company having made great efforts to advertise the project and consented to give up their rights as to the French river section, I think that, as my hon. friend as said, we are moving in the right direction.

How are they .going to get out from the Georgian Bay ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC \\ GRKS. By the clause that has been added the company has no right whatever on the French river except upon Order in Council. The French river does not form part of the Bill to-day. Now the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) says we must have control of the rates, that if the Ottawa and Mattawa part of the scheme fall into the hands of a private corporation we will not have control of the rates. Let me tell him that we have control of the rates by this Bill to a certain extent, and let me remind him that the government have in their hands the French river part of the scheme. We are altogether masters of the situation. My hon. friend knows better than any one else in tlie House perhaps that we must not rely on waterways only. I for one have the greatest confidence in railways and waterways combined. For instance, Buffalo is tlie gateway of the great system of American railways leading to the American ports. Midland, North Bay, Collingwood, Owen Sound and other ports will be reservoirs of trade. I have no doubt whatever, speaking after giving the question the most careful consideration, that the very moment the government announce that the French river will be improved so as to have a depth of 20 feet, there will he at least twenty-five or thirty large lake boats built immediately. There is no doubt as to that. I may add more. The Grand Trunk Railway have fully made up their minds to settle in Midland and in Montreal. This means aD immediate and large addition to their carrying capacity on the lakes. The Grand Trunk Railway will settle in Midland to a very large extent. That does not mean that they will not carry trade elsewhere. But it has been suggested that the Canadian Pacific Railway and tlie Grand Trunk Railway might perhaps use part of the road from Midland to Peterborough so that the two great railways toight combine their efforts to take
down to the St. Lawrence as much freight as they possibly can.
Now my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier), who has just taken his seat, is right when lie says that we have not perhaps a right conception of the immense development in store for us. Last year our crop in the North-west Territories amounted to 100,000,000 bushels of grain. The French river and the ports of the Georgian Bay will in future not only handle the Canadian trade, but the American trade. We have the shortest route ; we have only to make it the best to get the immense quantity of trade flowing down the great St. Lawrence route. My hon. friend is annoyed, and perhaps rightly so, because he is taunted, not in a malicious manner, with being a Canadian Pacific Railway man. Let me tell him that it happens often to me to be taunted in tbe same way. Every time I have to stand by a waterway or a railway that is connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway I am called a Canadian pacific Railway man. I am not ashamed of the appellation, not by any means. I was a newspaper man in the Conservative parry ranks, and I may say that when that great scheme was first initiated-
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

I am not more ashamed of that than 1 am of being called a Canadian Pacific Railway man. 1 am perfectly prepared to stand by my past here, and my past in the Conservative party, as I am prepared to stand by what I am doing now. I am often taunted with being a Canadian Pacific Railway man. I believe no greater project has ever been carried out than the construction of tlie Canadian Pacific Railway, and I believe that to-day we must stand by our Canadian railways and we must stand by them to the last, in the face of the organization of these great American interests. I have stated on several occasions, and I say It again, that if the hon. Minister of Finance were in a position to invest in Canadian Tacific Railwav bonds at 4 per cent interest $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 of Canadian money, if we could get it for less than 3 per cent, it would be a first class investment, because it would make this country secure tlie control of that great national highway. I have said more than I intended. I did not expect to say so much. However, I feel that we should move in the right direction.
s lion. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) has not dealt with the crucial point.
What is it V
As to the advisability of allowing any encouragement to be given by parliament to a private company to I engage in what will be a great national
enterprise in connection with one of our public waterways passing right through the heart of the country. I think it would be a very great mistake.
1 thought I had dealt with that.
No.

I believe I have. A charter was granted in 1894 by a former parliament and it was renewed in 1898 by a former parliament. Now, we except from the charter part of that scheme which is more at hand, if I may speak in that way, because, please not to forget that with an expenditure of less than $5,000,000 we will be in the position to make a deep waterway from the Georgian Bay to Lake Nipissing. As to the other part, if the company go on with their work, and if parliament should make up its mind that it is the duty of the country to take possession of the work, clause 43 of the Act gives it power to do so.

Will the hon. Minister of Public Works say how he could control the rates by having control of the French river, because this canal would only go to Lake Nipissing on the one hand and to Montreal on the other, and it would have no connection directly with the Georgian Bay.

There will be nothing easier than to have control of the rates. Suppose that we improve the French river from Georgian bay to Lake Nipissing. Then, we will make connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, or any other railway that may be constructed there. There are only 317 nautical miles from Montreal to Lake Nipissing. People who say that the rates will be in the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway will be mistaken. If the Canadian Pacific Railway take advantage of their position, nothing would be easier than to build another railway. I might add that the Grand Trunk Railway has also a branch line from Callander to the city of Toronto, and in my opinion no other city, except Montreal, perhaps, would benefit more by the improvement of the French river than the city of Toronto.

I think the hon. minister misunderstood me. What I referred to was the control of rates on the canal, not the ordinary freight rates-the tolls that may be imposed upon tonnage passing through the canal.

The hon. minister has not dealt with a most important feature to which reference was made by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier). Enormous power privileges would be developed by the construction of that waterway, and if they become possessed by the company, it may be necessary in a few years that they shall be acquired by the government.
139 i

I think that when a company are ready to put $70,000,000 or $80,000,000 into the country without the government being called upon to do the work, even if it does include the water power, we ought not to say anything against it. If this country is not ready now to go into that project, and I think myself it is rather problematical, we should not discourage capitalists from undertaking the work. Even hon. members opposite, who are in favour of the development of these great waterways, as we all are, I think, would be rather staggered if it were proposed that the country should put $80,000,000 into this project. For myself, I am rather inclined to come to the conclusion that after all the rail way problem in this country will discount every other question. I would not stop capitalists from coming in and making use of our waterways and water powers, and investing $70,000,000 or $80,000,000 in developing them. Is the country or is the government any the poorer because our undeveloped water powers are utilized ? Is Canada any poorer because the power at Niagara Falls is being developed ? I trust the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) will not oppose a proposition which will result in the introduction of capital into the country.

There is no desire j>n my part to prevent the introduction of capital to develop the public works of this country, but this is a most important artery of communication, one of the great natural highways from Montreal to the Georgian Bay, and the question has been raised whether it is advisable in the public interest to allow a private company to get possession of privileges that it may cost an enormous sum to purchase in a few years from now. If that power can be developed with advantage to the people at large why should it not be developed in a year or two and owned by the government for the benefit of the people of Canada instead of allowing it to be developed by a private company ?

Does not my hon. friend know that all the water powers that he speaks of are under the control of the provincial parliament ? These water powers are not under our jurisdiction at all.
Mr. CLARKE If you incorporate this canal company the project becomes a work under the control and authority of the parliament of Canada.
You cannot take rights away from a local legislature.

There are no representatives in this House from any part of the Dominion of Canada who will more cordially co-operate with the government in any scheme of national transportation than the representatives from Toronto. None whatever.
Glad to hear it.
If the hon. gentleman had listened attentively to the sentiments expressed by the members for Toronto during the past five or six years, he would have been convinced of that fact long ago.
Let the Bill pass.

Before it passes, I wish to express my opinion, and it is this, that this country is big enough and wealthy enough to undertake that work and complete it as soon as necessary, if it be a national work, and no charter should be given to private capitalists for the purpose of constructing a work absolutely essential to the future prosperity 'of this country. It may be said that by some provision of the Bill the government may take over the work in ten or fifteen years from now. But to do so will eventually necessitate a much larger expenditure than if the work were undertaken by the government now, and carried to completion at the earliest possible moment.
Bill, as amended, reported, read the third time and passed.

House in committee on Bill (No. 98) to incorporate the Montreal Subway Company. -Mr. McCarthy.
On section 8,

Before this clause is adopted, I would like to say a word or two. We have a charter for the construction of a bridge, which has been several years on our statute-book, but the bridge never materialized. I have no doubt that the population of the city of Montreal and of the south shore would rather have a bridge than a subway. I was a little diffident regarding that subway, but as there is no probability of any bridge being constructed, I did not feel justified in opposing the granting of a charter for this subway. Of course, it is a new departure. Will it be feasible to carry vehicles and so on in such a subway ? The promoters of the Bill say that it will. In the committee yesterday I asked for a short delay so as to be able to consult some of the eminent financiers whose names appear on the Bill. I met one or two of them to-day, and they told me-especially Senator Mackay-that they fully expected that the scheme could be financed without the help of the government of Canada. I read today an interview in the Montreal papers to the same effect with Mr. Hogg, in which he says that the scheme is sure of being financed without any trouble whatever. That will be a new departure, because in the past Mr. CLARKE.	[DOT]
we have been in the habit of giving pretty large subsidies to undertakings of this kind, but the moment we find capitalists prepared to take such a strong stand, who have such confidence in the development of the country, especially of the city of Montreal, as to be able to tell us that they are prepared to go on with such a work without asking anything of the government, I have not a word to say against it, but wish them success, prosperity and happiness in their undertaking.
Am I correct in the understanding, from the explanation of the hon. Minister of Public Works, that this is intended to be a traffic subway as well as for railways ?
There will be two subways-one for the railroads and another one for vehicles. The vehicles will be carried, I understand, on electric cars.
If my memory is correct, I do not recollect any provision in the Bill for control by the government of traffic rates.
We will see that when the other clauses are read.

The lion. Minister of Public Works has often objected to our accepting newspaper reports as authority. If the report to which he refers to is true, it is very important. What grounds have we for supposing that that newspaper report is more correct than others.
On section 20, subsection (b) :
If the company fails to bona fide expend upon its undertaking within nine months after the approval of said plans and specifications a sum not less than $100,000.
The sum of $100,000 to be expended within nine months is a very small sum for such a large undertaking.
It was understood in the committee that that was to be expended cm actual work.

I move that it be changed to $200,000 in six months.
Mr. McCarthy. There is considerable objection to passing an amendment in this way after the Bill has been thorouglily considered in the Railway Committee. At first $50,000 was thought to be sufficient, then it was proposed that $100,000 should be expended in twelve months, and after considerable discussion a compromise was arrived at by making it $100,000 in nine months. The Minister of Public Works had left the committee before that. The government have adopted the principle that when a matter has been thoroughly dis-

cussed before tbe committee the committee's recommendation shall be adopted. Why should a different course be pursued in this instance ? The minister says that he is satisfied with the financial ability of the company, and when these men are willing to deposit $50,000 and to spend $100,000 in nine months putting their own money in the enterprise without asking any subsidy from the government I submit that they should not be asked for more than is asked from any other company. It seems to me that to ask the committee at this stage to amend what the committee has reported is not in accordance with precedent or with the policy of the government.

I haVe no intention to be unfair, far from it. No doubt an enterprise of this kind should only be put in the hands of strong men, and I saw Senator Mackay this afternoon, before making up my mind as to whether I would agree to this Bill or not. He told me that lie expected the whole thing would be financed without any help from the government. Under the circumstances, 1 diu' not want to be too exacting. We have been used to so much charter trafficking in Montreal, that I feel the necessity of being careful. In the committee yesterday I inquired whether some of those gentlemen, whose names were on the Bill had not lent their names, for we have found that men jfi|t as great have lent their names elsewhere. Every day during the last week or so we have been reading what has happened in New York, and we must provide against a recurrence of anything of the kind, but I do not want to compare the men whose names are on this Bill with those who have been mentioned in New York.	[DOT]
It is provided that $100,000 must be spent on the construction within a certain time ?
It was stated in the Railway Committee, and agreed to, that $100,000 would be spent bona fide on the construction.
That is agreed to, and any words which may be inserted to that effect would be satisfactory.

As that clause is worded, the money may be spent on fees or commissions or charges of that kind, and not on construction work at all, and you will be locking this enterprise up in the hands of these men for five years without compelling them to do a day's work on it during that time.

The amendment ought to lie read to the committee so that the committee may know that the words ordered to lie inserted by the Railway Committee are actually inserted in the Bill. I do not know how it is, but this is not the
first instance we have had of Bills reported by the It a ijjyay Committee coming before this House, and not containing all the amendments that were ordered by the committee. This is rather an important matter. The committee decided emphatically that the $100,000 should be spent on construction work and not on plans and specifications or other such work. We should see that the clause is so worded as to leave no doubt that the money is to be spent on actual construction, and I therefore ask that it be read before it passes through the committee.

As some reflections have been cast on some of the officials of the Railway Committee, I beg to say that 1 drafted all the amendments myself and read them twice to that committee, and they are in the Bill in exactly the same words as I used in my drafts. Before the hon. gentleman makes any charge of that sort against the Railway Committee or its officials, lie should know what he is speaking about or take it back. Those amendments whether satisfactory or not, are exactly as they were drawn and read twice to the Railway Committee. The words 'actual construction ' were put in the first amendment and appear there now. The hon. member for Ottawa suggested those words, and I put them in at his suggestion and they are there now.

I understood that the amendment was read without those words. If they are in the amendment, then it was a mistake of the Chairman not to have read them.

I would ask the right Iron, the First Minister if he has received any further despatch or document respecting the colonial conference from the imperial government or the right hon. the Secretary of the Colonies. I would like also to bring to the attention of the hon. the Minister of the Interior-
Oh.

I would like to call the attention of the right hon. the leader of the House to the fact that there has been very bad order in this House for the past six or seven days, particularly when lion, gentlemen on this side are speaking. I am as anxious to co-operate with

my right lion, friend as any one can be to prevent this House from degenerating into a bear garden, and the next tHie these interruptions occur, I shall move that the committee rise, as a protest against them. Or if they occur when the House is in session, I shall move the adjournment, as a like protest ; and I call on you. Mr. Speaker, to see that a little better order is kept in this House in the future than has been the case during the past week. I was about to direct the attention of the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) to a telegram which I have received which possibly pertains to his department. I do not understand it myself, and I am asking the question for information. It is dated at Forty Mile, is addressed to myself, and is as follows :
Miners anxious to kuow decision regarding Miller Creek concession. Wire.

The only matter to which this telegram can refer, I think, is a dispute as to a number of entries for claims upon a place called Miller Creek. I know it was before me some months ago, and has been pending in the department from time to time since then. I think a decision was given some time ago and communicated to the gold commissioner. I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) more definitely to-morrow, and I can have a despatch sent to the gold commissioner to-morrow, if necessary, which will clear the matter up.
And if the hon. minister will mention also that the matter was brought up in the House, it will make it unnecessary for me to communicate with the gentlemen who sent me the telegram.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to repeat the question he asked of me.

I wished to know whether or not the government have received from the imperial government or from the Colonial Secretary any further despatch or communication with respect to the conference to be held in London during the coming summer. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will remember that one of the communications laid before the House referred to a further despatch from the Colonial Secretary, but when the matter was last mentioned in the House the right hon. gentleman stated that no further despatch had been received.

I have not made any inquiries, but I think I am safe in saying that there has been no further communication. I received a communication from Lord Strathcona a few days ago, not dealing directly with conference^ but on the subject of the wheat and flour duties.

There is one other matter to which I desire to ask attention-a statement by a reporter in the New York ' Evening Post ' of yesterday, relating to communications between the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Dominion Securities Company. It begins :
An officer of the Dominion Securities Company, which controls the Cape Breton Railroad, expressed astonishment to-day that Mr. Blair, the Minister of Railways and Canals, made a partial denial that the Cape Breton Railroad had been awarded a subsidy.
'We have a document,* said this officer, 'with Mr. Blair's own signature attached, vouching tor the subsidy, and it is open to inspection to anybody desiring to look at it, including Mr. Blair himself. You will notice that he did not deny the thing flatly. It is a well-known fact that under the general statutes of Canada any railroad company is entitled to a subsidy of 53,200 per mile by complying with certain conditions. The Cape Breton Railroad complied with them, and it has received proper acknowledgment of the same from Mr. Blair, with the official seal of his department attached. I may also say that the railroad company was awarded a like subsidy of 53,200 a mile from the provincial government, and1 a part of this subsidy has already been paid to the company.
Then follow some further comments upon the position of the law on the subject of subsidies In Canada, with which I need not trouble the House at present. I would like to know whether the right h<jn. leader of the government is in a position to say whether or not this statement respecting the assurance given by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) as to the subsidy, is correct or not. The Minister of Railways and Canals is not present, but perhaps the Prime Minister may be able to give information at present, and I would like to have a statement if the right lion, gentleman is in a position to make one.
I do not exactly understand the question.

I think the statement as read represented the Minister of Railways and Canals as stating that there was no arrangement or contract between this government and the Capo Breton Extension Railway. But the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals never said that. On the contrary, be said-and I said also, as having know-edge of the fact-that we had granted a subsidy for thirty-five miles of that road from the Strait of Canso to the village of St. Peters,
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: By statute.

Yes, and I presume that a contract was signed, because it was authorized. What the Minister of Railways and Canals said was in denial of the statement that the parties had

subsidies for much larger schemes. He did not say that there was no contract. I have not seen the contract covering the subsidy for thirty-five miles, but I think X am safe in saying that such a contract was signed with the Oape Breton Extension Railway Company, and, I suppose, passed to the Dominion Securities Company. There is no contradiction between what has just been read and the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways.

I was not making any assertion with regard to the matter. but merely sought information. There is this statement on the part of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals :
I do not hesitate to say that the statements in it it re absolutely false in the main, and I base my statements ou this ground, that the Dominion government has given them a certain subsidy and promised them other subsidies.
That is the statement of his which seemed not quite consistent with what has been stated by this officer of the Dominion Securities Company to the reporter.
There can be no document but the statute.
The document referred to, I suppose, would be the contract for the thirty-five miles which is not disputed.
Was that mentioned in the debate by the Minister of Railways ?

I know that I mentioned it. I was aware that the subsidy had been authorized for this thirty-five miles and the scheme approved to that extent; and I assume that the contract was signed, though I have never seen it.

I am afraid that is hardly warranted by the fact so far as my knowledge goes. My experience is that the enumerators spent very little time in taking the, census, much less time than was spent in 1891.
There is no doubt of that, because we had a great many more enumerators.

Well, they must have had very little to do as there was less population. I know that it did not take them two minutes to do the work at my house. I really do not think the explanation of the minister accounts for the increased cost.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I want to draw the minister's attention to the fact that the census of South Leeds in 1891 cost $1,652, while that of 1901 cost $3,393, and that the population in 1891 was 24,185 and in 1901 22,449, or a decrease in the population, according to the census returns, of 1,736. I am satisfied that the census returns for South Leeds are not correct, and that the population has not decreased. "We had an enumeration of the town of Gananoque taken at the same time by the municipal assessors, and it showed 170 more than the number given by the census enumerators taken at practically the same time. According to the municipal census of the whole county the population, instead of having decreased, has increased. Therefore, I think this is a case in which the minister should

send a special officer to make an enumeration of tlie county as a test for the whole province. I know that our county has not gone back in the last ten years, but has gone ahead. The cost of taking the census of the county in 1901 was more than double what it was in 1891, the increase being $1,741 with an apparently decreased population. The minister says the increase of the cost is due to an increased schedule of rates. The old rate to the enumerators was three cents per name, and the hon. gentleman allowed five cents, a difference of two cents. On the population of 22,449 this would give $448. Deduct that from the $1,741, the increase in the cost over 1891, and there is still an increase of $1,300. How does the hon. minister account for that V

The hon. gentleman has stated in the first place that the municipal census of South |I.eeds was greater in 1901 than it was in 1891, but if the hon. gentleman will look at the correct figures he will find that that is not the case. By the municipal census the population of the district of South Leeds in 1891 was 20,191, while in 1901 it was 19,193, a decrease of about 1,000. According to the Dominion census the population in 1891 was 22,449 and in 1901, 21,185, or a decrease of about 1,300, showing that the municipal census was not so very far different from the Dominion census. It is not correct, as the hon. gentleman states, that there was a decrease according to the one and an increase according to the other. With regard to the increase in the cost, the hon. gentleman has forgotten that the schedule of rates included not only five cents per name, but deaths, all farms recorded, thirty cents per industrial establishment instead of twenty, besides $1.50 per day which was allowed to the enumerators in 1901 for team hire and not allowed in 1891.

From the Bureau of Statistics.

I would like to know why it is that in taking the population of West Elgin the minister makes out that in 1901 it had 730 fewer souls than in 1891, while it cost $2,137.08 more than in 1891 to take the census.
The same explanation applies to that county which I have given for the others.
I did not catch the explanation. What was it ?

I can repeat it, I suppose; but I do not think it is necessary for me to go over the same tiling for every county in the Dominion. The explanation is simply that the schedule rates were higher in 1901 than they were in 1891, and the enumerators were paid by the schedule rates.

House in committee on Bill (No. 11) to provide for the establishment of a medical council in Canada.-Mr. Roddick.

I beg to suggest the following amendment to subsection 3, of
section 6 :
No province shall be represented on the council either by appointed or elected members until the legislature of the province has enacted in effect that registration by the council shall be accepted as equivalent to registration fOT a like purpose under the laws of the province provided that when all the provinces of the Dominion shall have legislated in effect as aforesaid, it shall be lawful to appoint and elect Jn the manner aforesaid members of the council representing the provinces which have so legislated, and the universities and- incorporated schools aforesaid constituted within such provinces and such members shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, constitute the council.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roddick) please explain his amendment ?

The original clause provided that when any five or more prov'nces had legislated, this would come into effect; the amendment provides that all the provinces .shall legislate before the council can be formed.
We are anxious to know if this medical council will come into existence if one of the provinces refuses to join ?
No, they must all join before it can come into operation.

Therefore, the hon. gentleman admits by this amendment that this parliament has not authority to pass such legislation, but he must have the authority of a provincial legislature. Why, then, should we pass this Bill ? SVhy not leave the matter to the provincial legislatures 1 This is the first time I have seen such a Bill passed by this House. It is an invasion of provincial rights, and the promoter practically admits it by this amendment.

I do not think that is a fair interpretation of the matter. The mere leaving of the right in the hands of the provinces to come in or not is not an acknowledgment that this parliament has not the power to legislate on the subject. It is acting in an agreeable way towards

the provinces, when they are neither forced nor asked to come in, but allowed to come in of their own free will.

This arranges a piece of machinery which the provinces can make use of in order to establish a council. The provinces cannot do it themselves. This parliament simply arranges a scheme by which they can get together and establish a council which will issue licenses and allow any licentiate to practice in any part of the Dominion. Then we shall be able to have reciprocal legislation with foreign countries which is very important.

In my judgment this legislation should originate with the imperial parliament and not here. You are practically amending the British North America Act. We can understand this better toy referring to a point which was explained here by my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Russell). It is provided in the British North America Act that the different provinces of the Dominion can have legislative union, with the exception of the province of Quebec, but, before this legislative union* fakes place, the consent of the different legislatures must toe had. This was passed toy the imperial parliament in 1867. But there is nothing of that kind as to the medical profession. On the contrary, that is a civil right which belongs to the different provinces. I would toe very happy to support this legislation, because I think that the motives of my hon, friend are good motives indeed, but that it is an invasion of provincial rights. By the revised statutes of the province of Quebec, clause 3975, the medical profession comes under our provincial law. There is nothing in our constitutional Act providing that this parliament can legislate in matters of that kind. I most humbly protest against this legislation. I say it is not within the purview of this parliament, and I say that if we pass such legislation, we open the door t* many other Acts of the same kind.

If I thought that this Bill infringed on any provincial rights, I would be as. strenuously opposed to it as any hon. member of this House. As a matter of fact, I have, on various occasions during the present session raised the point with regard to measures before this House, and pointed out that these Bills should be dealt with by the provincial legislature, and I have not received any support in these matters from the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux). This docs not seeim to me to infringe in any way upon provincial rights. There is no provincial legislature in Canada that could enact a Bill of this kind-my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) would not pretend that there
is.	The object of the Bill, as I understand
it.	is. with the consent of the legislatures of the provinces, insofar as they have exclusive jurisdiction, to provide a scheme
by which medical practitioners in Canada shall have, in Canada as well as in foreign countries, a Dominion status and not a merely provincial status.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) allow me to ask him a question V Is it not a fact that by this amendment the promoter of the Bill admits that the provinces alone are entitled to legislate in this matter ?

If my hon. friend will define what he means by ' in this matter ' I can answer him with greater precision. But, so far as the scheme of this Bill is concerned, my answer to his question is an emphatic negative. The rights of the provinces in ithe matter of property, and civil rights are conserved by the amendment that my hon. friend (Mr. Roddick) has introduced. The creation of a council which, with the approval of the provincial legislatures shall have the right to deal with the medical profession of the various provinces is attempted by this Bill and can only be dealt with by this parliament. That is a scheme which can only be dealt with by some such Bill as this, and can only be carried out with the consent of the provincial 'legislatures, and in every way this Bill safeguards provincial rights toy providing, as this amendment provides, that the medical profession in the provinces cannot be affected except with the consent of the legislatures of all the provinces. Further than that, this council shall not be created at all unless every province of Canada comes into the scheme. That is the idea of the amendment, as I gathered from hearing it read. Now it does not seem to me that under these circumstances there can be any objection to this Bill from the standpoint of provincial rights. If I thought there was such an objection, I would be the til-sit to stand -up and support my hon. friend, because I for one am as anxious that provincial rights and the federal constitution should be preserved intact in every respect as any hon. member on either side of the House can possibly be.

With reference to the amendment that the committee has just adopted, would it not be advisable to provide in the Bill some way of determining whether the various legislatures have given the consent that the Bill requires before this Act can go into effect ? There is no tribunal to determine whether the provincial legislation contemplated has or has not been enacted.
That is implied in the word * legislation.'

The words of the legislation are not set fortn here. Whilst it says that the legislation shall be to a certain effect, yet it will be a question whether it was to that effect.

You might proceed to establish your schools and purport to grant licenses, and after all, oil the matter being tested, it might be held that one or other of the supposed provincial Acts did not comply with the conditions of this measure.
The Governor in Council will determine whether the necessary legislation has taken place.
Where is it stated that this legislation shall not go into affect until it is assented to toy all the provinces ?
That is provided for by the amendment which has just been adopted.
Then are we to understand that all the provinces must consent V

Yes. I have amended the Bill so as to make it impossible for five provinces to begin this work, they must ail consent before the council is formed. If one does not consent, it cannot go on.
