Mr. RODDICK moved the second reading of the Bill.

Before the Bill is carried, I must say that I was absent when the second reading was taken, and I have only this opportunity of making some observations against the principle of the Bill. However, I do not regret to have been absent at the time, because the amendment that has just been adopted by the committee gives a special feature to the Bill which I think is an argument against the Bill itself. In taking exception to the principle of the Bill I do not do so from a professional point of view. I am not a medical man, and those medical men in my county whom I represent here are practically all in favour of the Bill, because they live on the border of the province of Ontario and they would certainly benefit by the adoption of this Bill. My objection is entirely based upon the principle of the Bill which was pointed out by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux), a few moments ago. Now I am not a lawyer any more than I am a physician ; but I think we must admit that common sense tells us that what belongs to the provinces does not belong to the federal authority, and what comes under the federal authority does not come under the provincial authority.
That may be common sense but it is not law.
And gentlemen who do not belong to the noble profession of the law will admit that sometimes lawyers attempt to justify things that are not common sense.
That depends on the common sense.

But it is the habit of those gentlemen to play with common sense when it suits their purpose. It is a principle admitted in law, a principle that 1 think the very high authority of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will not contradict, that whatever power belongs to the provinces belongs to them toy the authority of the imperial government. This parliament cannot give them one iota of authority, this parliament cannot authorize the provinces to legislate on any subject. Whatever authority the provinces have to legislate is given to them by the imperial parliament, and whatever power is given to us is given toy the imperial parliament. We are imperialists in this sense, that we respect what is given to us by the imperial power. So far as that is concerned I am a sound imperialist But if we want to have peace in this country we must leave the line of demarcation between the provinces and the Dominion authority perfectly well defined. Now I have had occasion in this House to speak against some measures of the government where I thought they were not exercising the full power given to the federal authority, and were giving to the provinces power that did not belong to them.
You voted all right.

No, I voted against them, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) voted with the government at that time because his leader told him to vote with the government-I mean on the Manitoba railway legislation.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) pardon me ? Is he referring to me 1
I am not quite sure when the authority of the hon. gentleman began.

I was merely suggesting that if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) referred to me as having directed any one to vote for the Manitoba Bill, or as having said a word about it, he is stating what he cannot know to be true and which is absolutely and wholly untrue and incorrect.

I did not mean to insinuate that tlie hon. gentleman had given the word to the hon. member (Mr. Cochrane). I am sure that the docility of the hon. gentleman is such that he votes before the order comes from his leader. The ground that I am standing upon is that this very amendment which has been proposed by the promoter of the Bill and adopted by the committee is an acknowledgment that the provinces have the right to legislate in this matter. Now. the hon. leader of the opposition says that we do not encroach upon the authority of the provinces in this Bill. What do I read in section 4 of this Bill ?
I may say to my hon. friend that outside of the empire arrangements may be made with other countries. Reciprocity with France is quite possible.

As far as this part of tlie project of the hon. gentleman is concerned, I am opposed to it also. Whether the reciprocity is with England or with France, or with any other country, I say that we should not open the door to an exchange of that kind. We should not in the interests of the Canadian people encourage our medical men to go and live in other countries and lie replaced by foreigners. We know that in England, as well as in France, they are overcrowded more than we are with young practitioners who would he very glad to come here and invade this country, not with tlie greatest benefit to this country. After all, the very argument that will be used by these gentlemen will be that we are not satisfied with the courses that are given by our universities, that we are not satisfied with the studies pursued in our universities, and that we want to have reciprocity so as to invite foreigners to come and take the places of our practitioners. I may say that this view was expressed to me by a couple of physicians from the city of Toronto. Unfortunately, I did not think that I was going to take part in this discussion, and I did not obtain permission to give their names; but they are practitioners who have lived in England as well as here and they told me they were opposed to this Bill on tlie very ground that is taken by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roddick), i.e., that it will bring a taint reciprocity ; because they believe that reciprocity will certainly turn against the medical profession of Canada much more than it will turn in their favour.
But apart from this objection, I say that we cannot accept the principle of this Bill without either encroaching upon provincial rights or stultifying ourselves. Without the amendment which lias been proposed by tlie hon. member, we are encroaching on provincial rights in legislating upon a matter which lias been acknowledged as being the sole right of the provinces to deal with.

Under the amendment proposed by the hou. gentleman, we are simply stultifying ourselves. Either this legislation is good or it is not; either it is within our right to pass it or it is not.	If this legislation is
good, let us have the courage to pass ft. If it is our right to pass it, let us take the responsibility of it, and not say that we are passing legislation but that it is sham legislation, which will not come into force until all the provinces have adopted it. In respect to the argument used by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), that it is simply a matter of politeness, I would ask if we are here to pass laws for politeness ? Let parliament take the responsibility of saying for the first time that we have the right to legislate upon the medical profession ; and next year we will be called upon to legislate upon the legal profession, and the next year after we will be called upon to legislate upon other professions, and we will be encroaching upon provincial rights.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) if there is not a provision in the British North America Act under which we might legislate in re-' gard to the provinces and their laws, and whether this legislation might not come in under that section V

I am very glad that the hon. gentleman has raised that argument. Section 94 of the British North America Act says :
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, tho parliament of Canada may make provision for the uniformity of all or any of the laws relative to property and civil rights in Ontario. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and of the procedure of all or any of the courts in those three provinces, and from and after the passing of any Act in that behalf, the power of the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to any matter comprised in any such Act shall, notwithstanding anything in this Act, be unrestricted ; but any Act of the parliament of Canada making provision for such uniformity shall not have effect in any province unless and until it. is adopted and enacted as law by the legislature thereof.
By this clause the right was given to this parliament to legislate as far as the three English speaking provinces are concerned, provided it was ratified afterwards by the parliaments of these provinces. Now. in the amendment which has been accepted by the hon. member (Mr. Roddick), the spirit of this clause, which does not touch the province of Quebec, is made applicable to legislation which invades practically the rights of Quebec out of the fundamental provinces in the Dominion. Therefore this is an abuse of this clause of the British North America Act, which was introduced for the protection of the province of Quebec, and it is used against the will of the majority of the medical men of that province. It may be said that the province of Quebec 1
lias the right to resist this legislation through its provincial parliament, but I say that we should not put any provincial parliament in that position. I presume that this amendment has been suggested by the government in order to smooth differences of opinion: in order to prevent anv province from resenting this legislation. Well, either the people of the province of Quebec are in favour of this, or they are not. If they are in favour of it, why not adopt the legislation as it was ? and if they are not iii favour of it, and if this amendment has been proposed in order to smooth their feelings, what will be the result ? Most probably the other provinces will ratify this legislation and you will put the legislature of the province of Quebec in the unfortunate position of forcing it to resist legislation that has been adopted, first by tile federal parliament and then by the other provinces. The resentment which may be entertained in the other provinces will certainly he greater than it would be if this government had the courage to say that, we cannot adopt this legislation because it is against the spirit of the constitution. That is the view I take of this matter, and that is why I oppose the third reading of this Bill. I repeat that we should be careful to keep our legislation on the right track, so far as the autonomy of the provinces is concerned. If any of the provincial parliaments proposed to encroach on the powers of this federal parliament, I would say :	Let us stand by the federal power
and resist the province In spite of whatever unpopularity we may be subject to in a particular province. But, let us also stand by the provinces when they are within the constitution, and not invade their power. If we pass any such legislation as this we are" opening the door to friction between the provincial and federal authorities, and we are not discharging our duty to the people of this country. Whatever may he the practical advantage of any such legislation, we must learn to make sacrifices so as to maintain the spirit of our constitution. This Bill is against the spirit of our constitution, and it is for that reason that I shall vote against it.

My hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) has told this House on former occasions, that he did not believe much in logic, and lie has given us an example to-night which indicates in the str ngest possible manner the truth of that assertion. The hon. gentleman says that the provincial parliaments should not be called upon to confer any rights upon a body constituted by this parliament, and that the line of division between the federal parliament and the provincial parliaments must be kept absolutely separate and distinct. I supp:se that if what my hon. friend has argued is correct, exactly the converse must be true ; and yet the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) supported by his vote a Bill introduced by the govern-

ment which appointed provincial officers as the persons who should regulate the electoral lists under which members are returned to this parliament. Does not my hon. friend see that if he supports legislation of that kind, it is just as competent for a provincial legislature to confer upon a body constituted by this parliament power to make regulations with respect to matters under provincial control. Does my hon. friend admit that or does he not ?
Does the hon. gentleman refer to the Franchise Act ?
I do.

The great difference is that by the Franchise Act we did not give the provinces the right to legislate as to our franchise. We chose out of our own free will to use the provincial lists, and if to-morrow we want to adopt a federal franchise we can do so. If a provincial government had enacted-and it would be absurd for them to do so-that certain lists should be used for federal purposes, then I would be opposed to it.

I do not understand the distinction that the hon. gentleman has made. This parliament with the assent of the hon. gentleman conferred upon provincial officers, appointed under provincial laws, the power to select the persons who are to elect members to this parliament; a right which is absolutely possessed by this parliament in the first instance. This parliament delegated that duty to provincial officers, and it enacted it in such a way that provincial legislation regulating the electorate from time to time shall absolutely apply to the electorate who are to return members to the House of Commons. The hon. gentleman was not shocked by the delegation in that case, nor is he shocked every day in this House when we delegate power to the Governor in Council; nor is he shocked when provincial legislatures delegate their powers to municipal councils. But he conjures up a nightmare in this case because the effect of this Bill is to enable provincial legislatures to confer upon a council constituted by this parliament, power to make regulations respecting the medical profession in the different provinces. That is my hon. friend's logic. Does he or does he not think, that this parliament has the power to delegate certain powers to the Governor in Council ?
In (this case you advise the legislature.

In what way do we advise the legislature ? Even if it were so, is there anything in the British North America Act that says we should not advise the legislature ? How do we advise any more in this case than when we delegate most important powers to the Governor in Council ? Does not the hon.

gentleman know that provincial legislatures confer every day upon the Lieutenant Governor in Council and upon municipal councils, power to make certain regulations which when once made have the force of law. All that this Bill amounts to is, that with the consent of the provincial legislatures, and toy their enactment, a council shall be constituted which when it is once constituted shall have the power to make certain regulations with regard to the practice of the medical profession in the provinces. How can it be said that there is the slightest interference with provincial rights in this ? If you want an illustration of the carrying out of this very principle, look at the Canada Temperance Act, which is an example of the delegation of power of the most extraordinary character. We pass a law here and we say that it shall not go into effect until voted upon by the people of a particular locality. Examples of legislation of this character are so frequent that if my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) had only stopped to think for five minutes before he made his speech

Will the hon. gentleman pardon me. The hon. gentleman is now arguing about the delegation of powers which we have the right to recall. But in the present case it is a power that we are taking from' the provinces. The hon. gentleman has just stated that the provinces cannot legislate on such matters as we legislate upon. Suppose this Bill is passed by this House and is afterwards adopted by the provincial legislatures, does he say that the provincial legislatures afterwards could amend this Bill in any way, or repeal any part of the power we are taking in passing it ?
I should think that the studies of my hon. friend in constitutional law would have taught him that any legislature which has power to pass an Act has power also to repeal it.
Exactly. We have the power to repeal this Act, the provinces have not.

The provinces have the right to repeal any Act they have once passed, and no provision passed by this parliament could take away from any provincial legisl|ature that powerj for a single instant. If my hon. friend possessed the miost elementary knowledge, as I am sure he does possess a very great knowledge of constitutional law, he would understand that that is the case. If we desired by the mosit emphatic words in the world to override the right of a provincial legislature to repeal an Act it once passed, we could not do it. A moment's reflection would have shown my hon. friend that that is an elementary principle of constitutional law. In the face of that, how can it be contended that this Bill is an invasion of the rights of the provincial legislatures ? If I thought
4450

it was, I would be the first to oppose it. The scheme, in. a few words, is that this parliament, being the only legislative body that has the power to do so, shall create a council to regulate the medical profession in Canada. Under the amendment proposed by the mover of the Bill to-night, that council can only toe constituted by the assent of every province of Canada. Therefore every province oif Canada has the most absolute and complete control over this council, because any province can prevent it being constituted, or can make any regulations or qualifications with regard to it that it desires. It can do that just as freely after this Bill passes as it could before. My hou. friend hinted at some dark scheme on the pant of the mover of the Bill to begin an invasion of provincial rights, or spoke as if the Bill might be a mere cover for some attempt to invade provincial rights in the future. The scheme is one( which I would have thought would have provoked the support of a gentleman of the independence and broad-mindedness of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat. lie has told us himself that he is very independent in all these matters, and we are bound to believe him. In fact, I think he sometimes hints vaguely that he is the only really independent gentleman in this House, with possibly one or two exceptions-that every other member of the House is more or less bound up by some ties or mysterious influences which prevent him following the dictates of his conscience; but my hou. friend always claims for himself that he is wholly independent of ali such influences. That being the case, I would have supposed that my hou. friend would have looked at this Bill from this standpoint, that it was right that medical men in Canada-those of the great province from which he comes as well as those of the province of .which I come-ishould have something more than a provincial status; that they should stand before the world as tnen qualified to practice all over Canada; (that, having that status, they should have rights conceded to them all over the world, which, in some instances at least, they do not possess at the present time. Looking at the question from that standpoint, will not my hon. friend, who is fair in regard to all these matters, come to the conclusion that it is in the interest of the medical men of his own province as well as the medical men of every other province of Canada, that this object should be attained, and that the medical profession should not iu the future have a mere provincial status, but that, while preserving to their own province the rights 1 have mentioned, they should have the status of Canadian medical men rather than the status of mere provincial practitioners, having no rights outside of their own .province ? If my hon. friend looks at the matter with his usual fairness, and excludes from his mind this bogy of au attack on provincial rights, he 140

will really come to the conclusion that this Bill merits his support. I trust that my hon. friend will on reconsideration give it his support, and that it will pass unanimously.

(i) The qualifications to be required from all persons desirous of being registered, either as practitioners or students, under the authority of this Act, including the establishment, maintenance and effective conduct of examinations for ascertaining whether such persons possess the qualifications required ; the number, nature, times anU modes of such examinations.
What would the practical result of this legislation be, were it passed into law ? When this Bill is once passed and accepted by the provincial legislatures, the medical profession will come under the control of the Dominion parliament. AVhen the provinces have adopted this Bill, they will be dispossessed of the exercise of a right which they are now enjoying. As I said a little while ago, the subject-matter of this Bill is not within the purview of the powers of this parliament. The provincial legislatures having primary jurisdiction over educational matters and civil rights, we have no right to legislate here on these matters.
That tlie right to practice medicine is a civil right, and not a political right, is beyond dispute. Now, that is a subject-matter which is clearly beyond the jurisdiction of this parliament. And I say without any hesitation that, when the hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec have an opportunity to oppose such a legislation, they would prove false to their duty should tuey remain silent and fail to resist any encroachment on provincial autonomy.
This Bill, we are told, shall have no force, shall not become operative, until all the provinces have concurred, that is to say, until all the provinces of the Dominion, acting through their legislatures, shall have ratified this legislatiou. But we all know wnat a pressure will be brought to bear upon such provinces as may decline to adopt this legislatiou ; and it will he urged that the other provinces have taken it up and made it their own. They know that the province of Quebec is large-hearted ; that it was not like to lag In the rear ; and who would venture to say that one day it will not accept aud ratify that legislation ? It is on record tuat parliaments have sold their country ; and it would be no matter of surprise that the Quebec legislature should surrender one of Its rights.
Were I satisfied that this parliament is dealing with a subject-matter which properly comes within its jurisdiction, I would be quite ready to accept it.
It is urged that the medical profession is going to benefit by this Bill. 1 quite agree that it would be conducive to the good of the medical bodies, were graduates in medicine to receive a qualification to practice in more than one of the provinces. But the present state of things may be remedied by other means than the one suggested here. It lias not been shown that such a remedy as the one I am going to suggest would not apply to the medical profession. For instance, what has been done for the legal profession Mr. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville).
would also apply to the medical profession. There exists between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec an understanding under which barristers from one or the other province are allowed to practice their profession in those provinces, upon payment of the usual fee. Such a reciprocity has been brought about without any interference from the Dominion parliament. The conditions, however, were quite different. But the bars of Quebec and Ontario have come to an understanding, after having satisfied themselves that such reciprocity would be conducive to their mutual interests. For instance, not long ago the solicitor of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was admitted to the bar of tlie province of Quebec, without having had to pass any examination, and upon payment of the customary fee. The members of the legal profession did not come before this parliament to ask for the passage of such a legislation as is now under discussion.
Should the medical practitioners in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec come to a similar understanding, it could certainly be brought about without being sanctioned by this parliament.
On these several grounds, I move that this Bill be not read now, but this day six months.

It must be very gratifying to tlie promoter of this Bill to realize that so far the argument against the adoption of this measure has only been of a constitutional or legal character. I do not see that any argument has been made with regard to this Bill that Is detrimental to the practice of the profession. Some lion, gentlemen seem to fear that the medical profession will suffer if this Bill should come into operation. Legal difficulties have operated upon their minds and created the fear that the measure could not be satisfactorily put into force. They ha ve raised the question of provincial rights, I think, with perhaps rather undue warmth, considering the amendment proposed, and which appears to be favourably received by tlie House. Certainly, while we all agree that provincial rights are of great importance and that we should be very careful not to infringe upon these rights by any legislation, such as might perhaps require the intervention of the courts to decide as to whether the law we might pass were ultra or iutra vires, It does seem to me that there may be almost too much of a fetish made of provincial rights. The amendment does away with the last vest-age of complaint on that ground. There surely can be no objection to tbe provinces willingly giving up any vestige of a right they may have for the general benefit of the whole community. This was recognized by the British North America Act in one particular, though not as fully perhaps us would be desirable. But at any rate the reasonableness of such a course has been

recognized by tlie British North America Act. The medical profession is in many ways the most liberal of all the professions. It is one, the practice of which is not at all bounded by provincial linets. The practice of medicine involves the whole science of life in all its most minute ramifications, and is therefore not of a provincial or even of a Dominion character, but rather of an international nature, and if by any wise legislation this parliament can assist in raising the medical profession beyond provincial limits and even introduce international features into medical education and practice, I believe that we will be advancing along the lines of modern progress. The idea that a certain amount of protection should be thrown around the medical profession of each province will not stand, I think, careful examination. This Bill, if passed by this House, will not go ini to. full operation for quite a period of time, because it must be considered and adopted by the various provincial legislatures before it can become effective, and there must consequently be negotiations between the promoters of the Bill and the various provincial medical bodies in order to bring about such provincial action. But I believe that once this Bill is adopted by this parliament the time will no doubt come when the practice and study of the medical profession will be placed upon a much higher basis than at present. It is not at all probable that the Dominion government will ever be called on to contribute financially towards medical instruction, but when this council is once established and the different provinces give up their provincial privileges in the matter of medical education and practice, it is quite possible that some great scientists and philanthropists in the future will be induced to contribute largely of their means to the promotion of medical and scientific education, and the council incorporated by this Bill will be in a position to receive gifts from such sources and utilize them for the promotion of higher scientific Instruction. We know what is taking place in the neighbouring republic, owing to the munificence of Mr. Carnegie, who has devoted $10,000,000 for the benefit of science, and has established, with the aid of Congress, a board of trustees to supervise the expenditure of that fund. No doubt there were some timid souls in the American Congress who feared that state rights might possibly be violated by congress incorporating a board of trustees to administer this fund, but I have no doubt that such advocates of state rights have by this time discovered that their fears were groundless. It is possible that this measure will lead to something of that kind being done in Canada in the future. At any rate I believe that this amendment, approved, if not introduced, by the mover of the Bill, will remove all ob.jecti ins of this kind, and that this measure, when carried into operation, will be a means of placing 140*
the medical profession of this country upon a higher and broader basis than it has hitherto occupied. It must be a matter of regret always to the able physicians of the various provinces who have made their mark in the profession, that they cannot move from one province to another to practice their art when circumstances require them to do so, and I believe that this Bill when adopted will be a powerful lever towards raising the medical profession as high as a Dominion institution as it stands to-day as a provincial institution. I think I may say, without fear of contradiction, that no body of men stands higher in the various provinces than the medical men. They are devoted to their profession and all their ambitions are for the advancement of that profession, and when the distinguished medical men of the various provinces are called to this council, I have no doubt that the rising medical men of the country will be induced to take a higher course and prosecute their studies in Europe where they can enjoy all the advantages given by the highest universities dn the world, and the result will	toe a	higher
standard for the medical profession of the Dominion as a whole, which will place it on a par with that same profession in such countries as Germany, England and France. Let me add that the promoter of the Bill deserves well of the body to which he belongs and of which he is so distinguished an ornament, for the persistence he has shown in pressing this measure forward to its present stage.

In view of certain remarks made a moment ago by my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), I think I ought to say to the House that he is labouring under a false impression when he thinks that the government have adopted this Bill. The government have done nothing of the kind. It is a public Bill, introduced by a private member, and the government have no policy with regard to it. But I may say that after having given a good deal of study to the matter, I have come to the conclusion that this is a measure which ought to be adopted. When its second reading was moved I noticed an objection made by my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers), to the effect that it was an infringement of provincial rights and therefore unconstitutional. I gave that point some attention and it appears to me that, to remove this objection, I need only refer to section three which provides
3. The persons from time to time appointed or elected, or otherwise being, under the provisions of this Vet, members of the Medical Council of Canada, are hereby constituted a corporation under the name of [DOT] The Medical Council of Canada.' hereinafter called ' the council.'
This suffices to show that we have jurisdiction in the matter and can pass the Bill.

Therefore, the technical objection made by several of my hon. friends behind me that this measure is beyond the power of this parliament and belongs exclusively to the provinces, cannot stand. But the real objection, which was not expressed but ought to have been taken, and which to some extent has been advanced by hon. members, is that it deals with a class of subjects which come exclusively within the jurisdiction of the local legislature. The question therefore resolves itself into whether it is expedient for us or not to pass this proposed legislation, which certainly we have the technical right to do. My hon. friend says the whole question is not whether we have the technical right or not, but whether it is expedient to pass a Bill of this kind, even though we should have the power to do so, since it deals with a clasis of subjects which properly come within the powers of the provincial legislature.
I noticed the argument, the very strong argument, of my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers). He said that we were removing the medical students fiom the control of the provinces and bringing them under the control of a corporation created by this parliament. This is a very fair question for debate. But, after all the only question is whether it is wise or unwise to pass such a measure as this. When the Bill was introduced, the point raised by my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville might properly have been taken; and. if the Bill had remained as it was when introduced, I would have supported the argument of my hon. friend and would have said that we should not interfere with the status of the medical students and with the rights properly belonging to the provinces. But, with the Bill as it is now, with the amendments which have been made declaring in so many words that this Bill, shall not come into effect until it has been ratified by all the provinces, how can that contention be maintained ? I am a staunch supporter of provincial rights, as is my hon. friend from Labelle. But I would be safe in saying that the provinces would never be interfered with if the Bills passed by this parliament had a rider attached to them that they must be ratified by the provinces. The hon. member for Labelle says that we are stultifying ourselves by passing a measure of this kind, by passing a law and leaving it inoperative until it is ratified by the provinces. In my estimation -and surely it must be clear to my hon. friend-there is no stultification of ourselves whatever. We have power to do a certain thing, but we say : We will not use that power absolutely, we will enact a law which we think ought to be passed, but will leave it to the provinces themselves to say whether they will be bound by it or not. But my hon. friend from Labelle evidently went further. Evidently he has something in his mind, which, knowing him Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
as I do, did not surprise me. He says : This is the first step in the invasion of provincial rights in a more or less disguised way; suppose that next year legislation of this kind is introduced to incorporate lawyers of the Dominion. If any one were to introduce legislation of that kind, I would vote against it. I virtually gave the reason for that a moment ago when I said the question was whether it was wise or unwise to pass this Bill. I think it would be unwise to pass such a Bill relating to the bars of the several provinces. And the reason is obvious. The laws of the different provinces are different. There are no two provinces with the same laws. Therefore, it would not conduce to any good object to unite the bars which are to administer the laws. But the laws of the medical profession are the same everywhere. There is no difference in the teaching of medicine and the practice of the profession-and a noble-profession it is-between one province and another. Therefore, I think it is conducive to the interest of mankind to have as few as possible of these corporate bodies which have laws against one another. Leaving the technical and theoretical question aside, my hon. friend knows that in this very city of Ottawa there is a rivalry between the practitioner in Hull and the practitioner in Ottawa. The man having a certificate from Ontario would not dare to go to the assistance of a man in Quebec, nor would one having a certificate from Quebec give advice to an unfortunate invalid in Ontario. If argument is needed to justify such a measure as this. I think it can be furnished by the contemplation of such a case-a case that is not merely hypothetical. but a matter of everyday reality. I am moved in this matter by considerations of the expediency of the Bill. But I would not support it without the amendment that has been made providing that the Bill shall come into effect only with the concurrence of the provinces. If even one province does not give its concurrence, then my hon. friend the promoter of the Bill says, the law shall remain inoperative. Under the circumstances, it appears to me that the danger which some of my hon. friends think they see does not really exist.
Moreover, I am influenced by another consideration, which I give to my friends and to the House at large. Aside from other considerations, I do not hesitate to say, as a member from the province of Quebec, that, in my opinion, we would be warranted in supporting the Bill by the fact that there is no province that would profit so much by this measure as the province of Quebec. In my province we furnish a larger proportion of professional men than other provinces. There are French groups in all the provinces of the Dominion, and young men educated in the province of Quebec would be able, if this measure were in force to practice their profession amongst those groups. I do

not care very much-and In this I share the view of my hon. friend from Labelle-for reciprocity with other countries, but I care a great deal for reciprocity among the provinces of the Dominion. This argument, apart from all others, in my opinion, would be enough to warrant members of the House, and especially those from the province of Quebec, in supporting this Bill.

It would not be necessary for me to add anything to what the right hon. gentleman (Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has said, were it not for one statement made by my hon. friend from Labelle. The hon. gentleman said : If we wish to have peace in this country, let us respect each others rights. Well, I might add : If we wish to have peace in this country, for God's sake let us try to know each other better. I do not see what harm can come from scientific meetings among the members of the medical profession in this country. We do not take anything from the provinces by the Bill now under consideration, but simply provide machinery by which the provinces can, if they wish, form a body of medical men. If all the provinces do not agree, this body cannot be formed. My own opinion is that the province of Quebec will cheerfully agree to the Bill. I have reason to know that medical men of the highest standing in the city of Monreal-I speak of men of my own race-are in favour of this Bill, I am for the rights of the provinces, but I am also for the broader rights of this Dominion. There is no reason why Canadians should not work together wherever they can do so without invading each other's rights; and in this case, 1 do not think there is any invasion of rights or any danger of it. We must not exaggerate the rights of the provinces. My hon. friend from Labelle, who is a student of history, does not forget, I am sure, that it was the exaggeration of state rights in the United States which created [DOT] their trouble. We must not exaggerate provincial rights. We are bound, after all, to live together here ; let us not be afraid, then, to meet each other face to face, especially on the ground of science. A French Canadian physician is quite able to hold his own against any physician of any other race. I, for one, am not afraid of this Bill, far from it. As the Prime Minister has remarked, when this Bill has gone into force, you will see French Canadian doctors practising their profession in the other provinces more freely than they are doing now.

This Bill is being opposed by a certain number of gentlemen on this side of the House on the ground that it constitutes an infringement of what they call provincial rights. Now, I am one of those who do not believe in the cry of wolf, that provincial rights
are being invaded. I think we ought to resist any attempt to invade them; but I certainly do not think that we ought to cry wolf when the wolf is not in sight. I think that remark applies to the present case. There is absolutely no attempt to invade provincial rights by this Bill; and I am sure if my hon. friends, instead of reading only one clause of the Bill had read it in its entirety and had construed each clause by the others, they would have perceived that this Bill is nothing more or less than an enactment by this parliament that constitutes an invitation to the provincial legislatures to co-operate with us fully to occupy a ground that neither alone can occupy completely. Now, my hon. friends talk of provincial legislatures having exclusive rights. The provincial legislatures and the federal parliament have exclusive rights, but there is a common ground that both can occupy. There is no question better settled in this country by those who have studied law, than that any provincial legislature may occupy a ground of legislation until such time as the Dominion parliament steps in and takes the place of the provincial legislature. Take the ease of insolvency legislation, for instance. The point was settled beyond dispute by the Imperial Privy Council that the Ontario legislature had the right to legislate with respect to bankruptcy; but the Privy Council said : You have right to legislate with respect to bankruptcy until such times as the ground is taken up by the federal parliament; only until then. So there is a common ground that both the legislature and the parliament may occupy.
Something was said about legislation bydelegation. Now, about the time that the case of the Queen and Hodges was decided it is undoubted that there was some difference of opinion among the judges of this country as to whether a body could legislate by delegation. But there never was a time when there was any doubt that you could legislate by reference. Take a case that comes up here every day, a case well known to all, the jury system in a province. You have in the Criminal Code a clause which declares that the provincial jury system shall be applicable to criminal cases. If there is one thing we have a right to do, it is to legislate here with respect to criminal procedure. But we adopt provincial legislation with respect to the jury system and we make it our own. That is what is called legislation by reference, that is not legislation by delegation. Legislation by delegation is that which the leader of the opposition spoke of a moment ago, for instance, that with respect to municipalities. However, I do not propose to discuss this at great length, because it is a very easy matter to make a cheap display of knowledge in a matter of this sort.

Now, if we make this legislation dependent upon the action of the provincial legislatures, Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.

An attempt was made a moment ago to make a comparison between this legislation and the provision of the British North America Act, which has reference to uniformity of laws; and my hon. friend confused the matter by saying that the British North America Act provided for the unification of the bar. There is no reference of that sort in the British North America Act, there is no reference to the bar. But in this section 94, which is a special section, provision is made for a departure from the whole scheme of the British North America Act. The whole scheme of the British North America Act is that the legislature shall have exclusive control over laws affecting property and civil rights in the province. But section 94, which is a departure from that, provides that with respect to some of the provinces there can be uniformity of law. But that is not what we are attempting to do here at all. The Bill is in effect a proposal carefully thought out constituting nothing more than an invitation to the provinces to legislate to adopt the qualifications to be established by the Dominion council. It is quite optional with each of the provinces whether it will accept this invitation or not, so long as any province does rot legislate in the manner necessary to supplement the provisions of this Bill it cannot be in any wise affected by the Bill. It is certain that the proposal, *n order to have any effective result as to any province requires joint legislation hy the Dominion and the province. The Bill is an attemi.it perfectly constitutional and legal, I think, t.o give effect to a scheme which owing to what may be termed the defects of the federal system cannot come into operation except by joint action.

I hope the House will pardon, me if I trespass at this late hour by taking up a few moments in discussing one aspect of the Bill which has not been referred to at any great length before. Whilst I am prepared to support the Bill on the general and broad grounds so well given to the House by the right bon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Eaurier) and other bon. gentlemen who followed him, and whilst I agi-ee entirely with those grounds as well as with the ground that this Bill is absolutely constitutional and within the power of this House to enact, I want to point out to some of my hon. friends from the province of Quebec that in looking at this question they are doing it exclusively from the point of view of some of the French Canadians of that province. I want to look at it from the point of view of the French Canadians in the province of Ontario, for whom I think I have some warrant to speak, as I am one of the trwo representatives of the French Canadians in the province of Ontario. I think I voice

the feeling of the 250,000 French Canadians in the province of Ontario, when I say that they are desirous of having medical men of their own tongue to minister to their wants in case of illness, and that this Bill is going to confer a great boon upon them. Much difficulty has been experienced in the pasit on many occasions in securing the aid of such medical men in the city of Ottawa, and the difficulty has not been confined to the city of Ottawa. It has been experienced all along the Ottawa river, and all along the boundary line between the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario. People living on either side of the boundary line have not been able to secure the services of medical gentlemen living on the opposite side. To my own knowledge for several years past a number of medical men have come to Ottawa from the province of Quebec with the intention of practising their profession. Because they wore not sufficiently familiar with the English language they have found difficulty in passing the examination necessary before they are permitted to practice in this province, and these gentlemen after one or two unsuccessful attempts to pass this examination have gone back to the province of Quebec.
That is not a compliment. All the members of the medical profession in the province of Quebec speak both languages.

I do not agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux). I may say that there are many who are able to speak both languages who would find difficulty in undergoing a technical examination in English. I do not think that in saying that I cast any reflection upon the medical gentlemen of the province of Quebec; or upon their scientific or literary attainments. The number of French Canadian doctors in the province of Ontario is altogether inadequate to the wants of the French Canadians who live in this province. In view of that fact, I hope that this Bill will be adopted

Mr. Speaker, I wish to explain why I am compelled, as 1 am compelled, to vote in favour of the amendment. I regret exceedingly if the vote which I feel obliged to give on this occasion should be interpreted as being in any way hostile to any well-directed movement made in this country in favour of broadening our Canadianism. I appreciated very much the remarks made by the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and by his colleagues, and I appreciate the motive of the hon. member for Montreal, Sit. Antoine (Mr. Roddick). Referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) who spoke for the inhabitants of one end of the province of Quebec and also of the adjoining portion of the province of Ontario, I may say that I represent a constituency situated
at the other end of the province of Quebec, which occupies towards the province of New Brunswick the same position that this portion of the province of Quebec occupies towards Ontario. I have come to the conclusion that under the circumstances we have not had produced either in this House, or before the special committee that was charged with the consideration of this Bill, an expression of opinion from the medical profession of the province of Quebec. I hold in my hand a memoir which was addressed to parliament by La Societe Medical e de Quebec in which they raise very serious objections to this Bill, and in which they state that through a misunderstanding they were unable to have their views placed before the committee. They very reasonably ask that this Bill be deferred until next session for further consideration. If the object to be attained is one to bring together all the medical men from the various provinces, I think that nothing should be done which would be of a nature to cause any friction between the various provinces. I have no difficulty in understanding that the English provinces of the Dominion will immediately accept this Bill, but the position of the province of Quebec is very different from that of the English provinces. Quebec has an educational system of its own. Its universities guide its classical studies. This medical council will, should this Act go into force and be ratified as it may be by the provincial legislature, have the power to control tlie curriculum of studies in the various educational institutions in Quebec.
Absolutely none.

I understand the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) to say absolutely none; but subsection (c) , clause 4, says that one of the purposes of the council is :
The determination and "fixing of the qualifications and conditions necessary for registration, including the courses of studies to be pursued1, the examinations to be undergone, and generally the requisites for registration.
Registration, where ?
Under the authority of this medical council.
Exactly.

But here is the position iu which this matter will stand twelve months hence if this Bill shall go through the House unopposed to-night and which the English provinces will accept :	Will the province of Quebec be
placed at the bar of public opinion in this Domiuiou, because, in trying to protect its own educational interests, it refuses to accept this law ? I do not say it will, but I do not think it is fair to the French province of this Dominion to put it in that

position. Like every otiler member of this House, I would like to see science make more rapid progress even than the wonderful strides it has made lately, but I do not wish this to be done at the expense of the good understanding and good feeling which should prevail between the various provinces of this Dominion. We have the example of the neighbouring states. In the neigbouring states no federal authority has attempted to legislate in the matter of medical diplomas. That power rests exclusively with each state which is one of the rights now enjoyed by the .provinces.
They are about arranging a scheme similar to ours, providing for a national council.

Well, the Americans are a very progressive people. If they have reached an arrangement of that kind in the United States, I do not say that it will not be reached in Canada, but my sincere conviction is that the immense majority of the medical practitioners in the province of Quebec are at this moment, and until they are convinced to the contrary, opposed to this Bill for the reason that the promoters have gone about it in the wrong way. They are trying to deal by federal authority with the question of education which is one of the sacred rights of the provinces, and for that reason, I consider it is my duty to vote in favour of the amendment.
